paragraphs.text: Long, long ago two boys were born on the same day in the same city. Tom Canty was born to a poor family, who couldn't afford another child. Prince Edward was born to a royal family, who welcomed the new heir to the throne.

A dozen years later, both boys lived by the river. While Edward lived in a magnificent palace, Tom lived in a shabby room in a poor neighborhood. While Edward's father was King Henry, Tom's father was John Canty, a thief. John often made Tom and his sister, Nancy, beg for money.

As Tom headed out to beg one January morning, he met Father Andrew. The priest had taught him how to read and write as well as some Latin. But what Tom liked best were Father Andrew's tales of palaces and princes.
"Do you have a story for me today, Father?" Tom asked.
"Of course!" the priest said as they walked together. "Once upon a time there was a prince named Richard . . ."
Because of Father Andrew's wonderful stories, Tom sometimes pretended to be a prince. This amused his friends, but they also enjoyed his game—except when he made them the servants.
All too soon Tom and Father Andrew arrived at the priest's church.
"We'll finish Prince Richard's story later," Father Andrew said.
"I can't wait!" Then Tom sighed. "It's time to ask strangers for money."
Tom hated begging, but his family needed the money. Most people ignored him, so he was surprised when someone tapped his shoulder later that day.
"What's this? A prince begging?"
Tom turned to find his best friend, Julian Witt, laughing.
"You have mocked royalty and are sentenced to prison!" Tom joked. Then, in his regular voice, he added, "I need a break. Let's see if anybody wants to play by the river."
Julian turned pale. "The river?"
"Oh, sorry! I forgot about what happened to you there. We'll stay away from the water today."
The boys found their friends, and the afternoon passed quickly. Prince Tom pardoned Julian, gave orders to his army, and met with his royal advisers.
"Your Highness, the sun is setting," Julian said.
"Oh no!" Tom gulped. "I have only one coin for my father!"
For a moment Tom thought about not going home, but he didn't want to miss supper. Reluctantly, he said good-bye and headed home.
"Where have you been?" Tom's father yelled. "You'd better have lots of money!"
"People weren't in a generous mood." Tom handed over his one coin.
"'A generous mood.'" John Canty echoed Tom's words. "Where do you learn this stuff? Probably from that priest."
That reminded Tom of something. "I wonder if Father Andrew has any books about Prince Richard," he thought. "Maybe I could—"
"Are you listening?" John shouted. "I said, go to bed!"
"Oh, don't send him to bed without supper," Tom's mother pleaded. Meanwhile Nancy tried to stay out of her father's way.
"Don't interfere!" John said to his wife. "To bed, Tom! Now!"

Tom went to a corner and untangled some old blankets. He made himself as comfortable as possible on the straw covering the wood floor. But for a long time, his hunger and his parents' arguing kept him awake. He tried to distract himself.
"How many princes has Father Andrew told me about?" Tom thought. "William, Richard, James . . ."
Tom drifted off, thinking of a distant kingdom. In his dream he was surrounded by lords and ladies, beautiful music, and delicious food. Everyone bowed to Prince Tom and obeyed his orders.
The next morning Tom awoke in the same filthy room on Offal Street. He was still hungry and still wearing his ragged clothes.
Tom sighed with disappointment. "I'll only be a prince in my dreams," he thought, slipping outside before anyone else woke up. "But maybe someday I'll meet a real one."
As Tom wandered along the river, he lost track of time and where he was. After a while he came upon a magnificent building.
Tom's eyes grew wide. "Could this be the king's palace?"

He joined a few people waiting near a golden gate. Suddenly a boy and a man appeared in the courtyard beyond the gate. Dressed in silk and velvet, the boy wore a sword at his hip. Tom heard the man call the boy "Your Highness."
"A prince!" Tom rushed forward for a better look.
Immediately a guard grabbed Tom's hand and jerked him away. "Step back, you pauper!"
The people laughed.
But the prince ran to the gate and scolded the guard. "How dare you treat a poor boy like that! Open the gate at once, and let him in!"
"You look hungry and tired," the prince said to Tom. "Come with me."
Tom was stunned by what was happening. The prince led him through the palace until they came to the prince's room. While the prince ordered breakfast for his guest, Tom looked around.
"Imagine sleeping in that big bed instead of on the floor!" Tom thought. "He has so many books and a suit of armor and—"
"What's your name and where do you live?" The prince interrupted Tom's thoughts.
"I'm Tom Canty from Offal Street. And who are you?"
"Prince Edward."
"Prince Edward! You mean, King Henry's son and heir?"
The prince nodded, and Tom quickly bowed. "I'm sorry to hear that the king is ill. Everyone is talking about him."
"I fear that my father may die soon. Some people say he's cruel, but he has always treated me fairly." The prince paused and smiled. "Though he does like to criticize me."
"My father is mean to everyone!" Tom said.
Just then Tom's meal arrived, and he dug in with both hands.
"He has no table manners," Prince Edward thought, "and yet . . ."
"You speak as though you've had some education," the prince said to Tom.
"Yes, I can read and write, but I struggle with Latin."
"Latin is hard at first," the prince said. "But enough about studying. Is it pleasant to live on Offal Street?"
Tom thought about the poor families who crowded together in every house. "Sometimes it is, but not when we're hungry." He gobbled up some ham and eggs.
"I hope that doesn't happen too often. Do you have any friends? What do you like to do?"
Tom swallowed some bread. "My friends and I are always racing to see who's the fastest."

"Oh, I'd like that!" the prince said. "People say I'm a good runner, but I don't have anyone to compete against. My only friends are my older sister, Princess Elizabeth, and my cousin, Lady Jane. What else do you do with your friends?"
"In summer we swim in the river. We shout and splash each other with water. Of course, that's after we've played in the mud and made mud pies!"
"I'm not allowed to get wet outdoors," the prince said sadly.
"Then how do you get clean?" Tom asked.
"I have many servants who help me bathe." The prince sighed. "Your life sounds wonderful. If I could run barefoot in the mud, I'd give up my right to be king!"
Tom was horrified. "You can't do that, sir! Besides, it's not all fun. On New Year's Day, my best friend, Julian, fell into the river and almost drowned. Luckily, a stranger saved him."
"I'm sorry to hear about Julian, but I wish I could play with your friends."
"And I wish I could be a prince, if only for one day."
"Would you really like that?" the prince asked.
Tom nodded.
Prince Edward grinned. "Then let's do it! We'll trade clothes for a while and then switch back before anyone finds out."

A few minutes later, the prince was wearing Tom's rags, and Tom was dressed in the prince's fine garments. The two boys stood side by side in front of a large mirror. They stared at each other, then at the mirror, then at each other again.
"We look so much alike," Edward whispered.
Tom laughed nervously. "We do indeed, sir."
"Except . . ." Edward frowned, peering at Tom's hand. "You have a bruise where that guard grabbed your hand."
"It's nothing." Tom hid his hand behind his back.
"It was cruel!" The prince stamped his foot. "Now close your eyes. I need to put away something important before I leave."
Tom didn't peek. He imagined that Edward was hiding documents—or even jewels.
"All done!" Edward said. "Don't move until I return to this room. That's a command!"
Tom stood still while Edward rushed from the room and out to the courtyard.
"Open this gate at once!" Edward shouted to the guard.
The guard hurried to open the gate. But as Edward passed by, the guard knocked him to the ground.
"You wretched pauper! Because of you, I got a scolding from Prince Edward!"
Edward's face flushed with anger as he picked himself up. "I'm Prince Edward! When I return, you'll be locked up for hurting me—and my friend!"
The guard sneered and gave Edward a mock salute. "I salute Your Gracious Highness. Now get out of here!"
A few people were still waiting outside the gate, hoping for a glimpse of royalty. They laughed and shouted.
"Make way for His Royal Highness!" they cried.
As Edward walked away from the palace, people continued to laugh whenever he called himself a prince. He continued to shout at them for not recognizing him as the heir to the throne.

At last everyone got bored and ignored him. By this time Edward's feet were sore, so he stopped to bathe them in a creek. Looking around, he recognized a nearby building. His father had turned it into a home for poor, abandoned children.

"My father has been generous to the children," Edward thought. "So I'll be treated kindly there." He looked down at his ragged clothes, which belonged to Tom, and sighed. "Right now I'm as poor as the children who live there."
Edward spotted a group of boys playing in a courtyard. They were all dressed alike in the school's uniform. The boys quickly gathered around Edward, who misinterpreted this as a sign of respect.
"Good lads," he said, "please tell whoever is in charge of this home that Prince Edward wishes to speak to him."
A loud shout went up, and the boys laughed at this stranger in rags.
"And who are you, beggar?" asked one boy, who seemed to be their leader. "The prince's messenger?"
"I am the prince! How dare you speak to me that way!" Edward was outraged because he was used to being obeyed, not insulted. His hand flew to his hip, but he found nothing there.
"Did you see that?" another boy asked. "He thought he had a sword just like a real prince!"
The boys laughed again.
Edward stood up tall. "You should be grateful that my father, the king, provides you with food and clothing. And you shouldn't be rude to me."
This made the boys laugh even louder.
"You are correct, Your Royal Highness," the first boy said. "Down on your knees, loyal subjects!"
Snickering and poking each other, the boys dropped to their knees and bowed their heads. Tired of being mocked, Edward kicked at the nearest boy.
"Take that!" he cried as he missed.
The group's mood instantly changed to anger.
"Throw him in the creek!" someone called out.

For a moment Edward was stunned. These boys were going to toss him in the water! Then he turned and ran as fast as he could. He didn't dare look back until he was far away. When he did, the boys were nowhere to be seen.
"It's a good thing I'm a fast runner." Edward smiled in spite of himself. "I could probably beat Tom Canty and his friends."
For the rest of the day, Edward wandered the streets, looking for Tom's house.
"If I can find Offal Street, Tom's family will realize that I'm the prince," he thought. "And they'll immediately take me back to the palace."

But as night fell, Edward was still out on the streets. He grew so tired and hungry that he could barely walk. He gave up asking for directions because everyone insulted him instead of helping him. After a while he stopped being angry with the boys at the children's home.
"Food and clothing are important, but they're not enough," he thought. "When I'm king, those boys will have an education too. And hopefully, they'll learn to be kind."
Edward pressed on as it began to rain and the wind picked up. He drifted deeper into the maze of filthy streets where the poor lived.
Suddenly a man grabbed Edward by the back of his neck.
"Got you!" he cried. "Out at this time of night, and I bet you don't have a penny to bring home. If that's not true, then my name's not John Canty, and I'll—"
"John Canty?" Edward twisted around to see the man's face. "Are you really John Canty? Then you must be his father! Take me back to the palace immediately."
" His father? The palace? I don't know what you're talking about. But I do know that I'm your father, and you'll soon regret—"

"I can't stand this a minute longer!" Edward cried. "Take me back to my father, King Henry, and he'll make you rich beyond your wildest dreams. Believe me, I'm telling the truth. I am Prince Edward, the heir to the throne. I'm not Tom!"
Confused, John stared at the boy. "I don't know what game you're playing, or if there's something wrong with your mind. But you're going home with me to Offal Street." He grabbed Edward again.
"Help me!" Edward cried as people passed by.
But John was already dragging the frantic, struggling boy toward Offal Street. A few curious onlookers followed them, but no one tried to help poor Edward.
Edward's first day as a pauper had not gone as he expected. How did Tom spend that same day? Left alone in Edward's room, Tom admired himself in the mirror and played with the prince's sword.
"I wish Julian could see me dressed up like this," Tom thought, grinning. "I look like a real prince!"
He sat on all the chairs and bounced on the bed. He knocked on the suit of armor but didn't dare to try it on. After half an hour, he was bored and lonely. He was also beginning to worry.
"Where's Prince Edward?" he thought. "If anyone catches me wearing his clothes, I'll be locked up in prison forever. I need to get out of here."
Tom quietly opened the door, and a servant sprang to his feet.
"Your Highness, may I help—"
Tom slammed the door shut. "That servant thinks I'm Prince Edward!"
Before he could decide what to do next, there was a knock at the door. The same servant entered and announced, "Lady Jane."
A girl in a beautiful dress ran toward Tom. But she stopped short when Tom fell to his knees.
"What's wrong, Your Highness?" she said.

"Have mercy on me!" Tom cried. "I'm not the prince, but only Tom Canty from Offal Street. Please help me find the prince and return these clothes to him. Then I'll be on my way and won't trouble any of you again."
"You shouldn't be on your knees, my cousin." Lady Jane was horrified. "I should be bowing to you."
She fled the room, which only increased Tom's panic.
"What should I do? What should I do?" he repeated, pacing the floor.
Meanwhile the servant told another servant what he had seen. "Prince Edward is behaving very strangely and doesn't think he's a prince!"
The news spread rapidly throughout the palace until it reached King Henry.
"The poor boy must be ill," he said.
King Henry immediately issued an order that all talk about Prince Edward's illness must stop. Anyone who disobeyed would be put to death. Then he asked for Prince Edward to be brought to him.

Tom didn't understand where Lord Hertford, the prince's chief adviser, was leading him. They walked down one long corridor after another. Finally, they entered a grand room, where an old man was lying on a couch. He sat up and beckoned for Tom to approach.
"My dear son, are you ill?" he said. "Or are you playing a joke on your father, the king?"
Tom instantly dropped to his knees. "You're King Henry? Then I'm in real trouble."
"Oh dear, I'd hoped the rumors about your illness weren't true," the king said. "But this is worse than I'd expected. Come here."
Trembling, Tom went and stood in front of King Henry.
"Prince Edward, tell me that you recognize your father," the king said.

Tom took a deep breath. "I hope that you'll believe me, Your Majesty, but I'm not Prince Edward. I'm only one of your subjects from the poorest part of the city. Please don't send me to prison. I'm too young to spend the rest of my life there."
"Send my son to prison? Don't be ridiculous," the king said.
Tom was relieved but still uncertain. "Then I'm free to go?"
"Go where?" King Henry asked.
"Home, Your Majesty."
Baffled, the king turned to Lord Hertford. "What do you think is the matter?"
"Perhaps only part of the prince's mind is confused. Your Majesty could ask him about something other than yourself," Lord Hertford suggested.
King Henry nodded and asked Tom a question in Latin. With some hesitation, Tom responded correctly.
"Excellent!" the king said. "Now try this." He asked another question in French.
"I'm sorry," Tom said, "but I don't even know what language you're speaking."

King Henry frowned. "Too much studying has obviously caused this problem, Lord Hertford! No more lessons for Prince Edward until his health returns. In the meantime," he said to Tom, "what have you done with the Great Seal?"
"The Great Seal?" Tom asked, confused.
"Yes, you wanted to look at it last week. But I need it so I can place my seal on the death warrant of the Duke of Norfolk. I would like my enemy to die before I do."
Tom bit his lip. "I have no idea where it is—or what it is."
"Perhaps Your Majesty could use the Small Seal," Lord Hertford suggested.
"Yes, yes, I know that." King Henry seemed tired and impatient. "Please leave."
Lord Hertford signaled for Tom to bow to the king.
"I'm a prisoner in this palace," Tom thought. "And I'll never be set free!"

5.title: Trying to Act Like a Prince

paragraphs.text: After Tom and Lord Hertford returned to the prince's room, some orders from King Henry arrived. Lord Hertford read the document before explaining it to Tom.

"Until you are well again, you must hide your illness," Lord Hertford said. "You must stop denying that you are Prince Edward. And you must stop talking about your family and home on Offal Street. They exist only in your imagination."
Lord Hertford rolled up the document. "If you don't recognize someone or remember how to act, ask me for help."
"If those are the king's orders, I must obey." Tom sighed and then looked at Lord Hertford curiously. "Why aren't you sitting down?"
"No one sits without your permission," Lord Hertford said.
At that moment Princess Elizabeth and Lady Jane were announced. As the girls passed Lord Hertford, he whispered, "Don't act surprised if the prince behaves strangely."
The girls giggled and exchanged looks before they curtsied to Tom. Despite Lord Hertford's warning, the conversation was awkward.
"Have you seen the queen today?" Princess Elizabeth asked Tom, after he invited them to sit.
"The queen . . ." Tom squeezed his eyes shut. He couldn't think of anything that Prince Edward had said about his mother. Suddenly he remembered why.
"That's because he didn't mention her!" Tom said aloud.
"Excuse me?" Princess Elizabeth said.
Tom looked at Lord Hertford for help, but his adviser merely groaned.
"I mean . . . that I haven't seen the queen yet." Tom fidgeted with the handle of his sword. "But I did speak to the king, and . . . he didn't mention her!"
Princess Elizabeth seemed satisfied with that answer. Tom flashed Lord Hertford a triumphant grin, and his adviser smiled weakly.
Lord Hertford decided to move the conversation away from the royal family. "The king has declared that the prince should take a break from studying," he said.
"That's a shame, but don't worry," Lady Jane said. "One day you'll be as wise as your father."
"Wise? He's an ignorant swine!" Tom scowled, thinking of his real father. Then seeing the horror in everyone's eyes, he tried to recover. "Um . . . well . . . what I meant was . . ."
Lord Hertford shook his head sadly.
"I didn't mean to insult the king!" Tom blurted out. "I'm not feeling well."
"We know that." Princess Elizabeth smiled politely. "You're not quite yourself today."
"That's for sure!" Tom thought, but he didn't say that aloud. Instead he said, "Thank you, dear sister, for being so kind and understanding."
For a few minutes, the conversation proceeded smoothly. But then Lady Jane said something to Tom in Greek.
"I have no idea what you just said." Tom felt his panic rise again. "I'm not sure that I can do this anymore. You see, I shouldn't even be here because I'm really Tom—"
Lord Hertford coughed loudly, and Tom realized he should stop talking. Lord Hertford pulled out a handkerchief and wiped some sweat from his face. He needed to put an end to this visit.
"My dear ladies," Lord Hertford said. "I hope you'll excuse His Highness because it's time for him to rest. The king doesn't want him to be tired for the banquet tonight."
"Banquet?" Tom's eyes opened wide. "What banquet?"
"You promised the king two weeks ago that you'd attend the mayor's banquet," Lord Hertford said.
"Oh, that banquet!" Tom smacked his forehead with his hand, pretending that he'd forgotten. "Yes, I must rest."
The girls stared at Tom, waiting for him to give them permission to go. Finally Princess Elizabeth said, "May we leave, Your Highness?"
"Yes." Then Tom remembered the way that princes spoke in Father Andrew's stories. "You are dismissed. May you have a good journey."
"A good journey?" Jane whispered as the girls headed for the door.
"He obviously has forgotten that we live here too," Elizabeth whispered back.
Tired from pretending to be a prince, Tom turned to Lord Hertford. "I really would like to rest now. You may leave."
Lord Hertford bowed and left the room.
But as soon as Tom flopped on the bed, a servant appeared.
"No, no, Your Highness," the servant said gently. "You can't sleep in those clothes."
Tom started to pull off his shoes, but the servant stopped him. "That's my job, sir."
A few minutes later, Tom was wrapped in a silk robe, but he couldn't sleep. When he opened his eyes, the servant was still standing by the door.
"What are you doing here?" Tom moaned.
"Waiting for you to dismiss me, Your Highness," the servant said with a smile.
At precisely one o'clock, the servant returned to wake Tom from his nap.
"Is there an outfit that Your Highness prefers to wear this afternoon?" the servant asked. "Or shall I choose something for you?"
"I'll just wear the same clothes I had on this morning." Tom got out of bed. "I usually wear the same thing all day, every day."
The servant tried to hide his surprise, but he shuffled his feet nervously. "Begging your pardon, sir, but you always change your clothes before lunch."
Tom laughed. "And I suppose I'll change into a third outfit before dinner?"
"Of course!" The servant relaxed, not realizing that Tom was joking. "You always change before dinner, especially for important events, such as the mayor's banquet this evening."

Tom had never owned new clothes, never mind more than one outfit. With the servant's help, he was soon dressed for the afternoon. He was then led into a large room, where some of the furniture was made of gold. In the center was a table set for one person. The heavy tablecloth was covered with food in silver dishes.
Tom sat down, eager to begin eating. But as he reached for a roll, a servant swooped in and tied a napkin around his neck.
"Oh, hello!" Tom said in surprise. "Who are you?"
"I'm the royal napkin holder, Your Highness," the man replied.
Tom inspected the napkin covering his clothes. It was made of snowy white fabric with lace edges.
"This is a beautiful napkin. In fact, it's too beautiful for a messy eater like me." Tom handed it back to the royal napkin holder. "Here, you take it. I'm afraid I'll get it dirty."
"Yes, sir." Behind Tom's back, the royal napkin holder raised his eyebrows to the other servants.
When Tom reached for a drink, he found that his cup was empty.
"My apologies, Your Highness." Another servant was holding a pitcher of water. "I didn't get a chance to fill your cup before you sat down."
"Who are you?" Tom asked.
"The royal cupbearer." The man beamed at Tom while pouring his drink.
Tom turned to see more servants.
"And who are you?" he asked another man and a woman.
"The royal taster." The man bowed low. "My job is to taste your food to be sure that it hasn't been poisoned."

"Well, if it were poisoned, it wouldn't be my fault!" A woman in a tall white hat gave the royal taster an annoyed look. "I'm the head chef, Your Highness, and I only serve food of the highest quality."
The royal taster ignored her and said to Tom, "I'm here to protect you from your enemies."
Tom gulped. "I have enemies?"
"Not many," the royal taster said. "You'll have more when you're king."
Tom gulped again. Then he pointed to a plate of brightly colored vegetables.
"What are these?" he asked the head chef.
"Your favorite vegetables, Your Highness." The head chef thought it was strange that he didn't recognize them. "You specifically requested cucumbers and carrots for today's lunch."
"Are these all my servants?" Tom asked Lord Hertford, who was standing and watching him.
"Oh no," Lord Hertford said. "You have 384 more, but don't worry about them now."

Tom turned back to his meal and dug in with his hands. The servants had been warned not to react to his strange behavior. But there was no danger that anyone would laugh. They all felt too sad about the changes in their beloved prince.
Observing Tom, Lord Hertford was puzzled.

"He walks like a prince and talks like a prince," Lord Hertford thought. "But it's odd that he doesn't recognize the king or any of his servants. He's completely forgotten how to behave—and his table manners are atrocious!"

Lord Hertford continued watching Tom. "It's also strange that he remembers Latin, but not Greek or French. He can't be an imposter because an imposter would insist that he's the prince. This boy has denied that he's Prince Edward."
Lord Hertford concluded that this must be Prince Edward, and something had gone terribly wrong with his mind.
After Tom finished his chocolate pudding and licked the bowl, there was one dish left on the table.
"Nuts!" Tom began filling his pockets with them.
Lord Hertford cleared his throat and frowned.
"That probably means I shouldn't do this," Tom thought. "But I don't care! I want to eat nuts in my room, where no one can watch me."
Suddenly Tom's nose started to itch. "I'm sure there are rules against a prince scratching his own nose too," he thought. "What should I do?"
Tom wanted to return to the prince's room and eat nuts. But first he had to deal with his itchy nose.

So he continued to sit at the table. He wrinkled his nose, trying to get rid of the annoying sensation. But that only made him want to sneeze. As Tom's eyes began to water, his distress became obvious to everyone in the room.
"Do you need some assistance, sir?" the royal taster asked. "Was there something wrong with the food?"
"There was nothing wrong with the food," the head chef snapped. "I sampled all the dishes myself before they were brought to the table. Everything was delicious!"
"Perhaps you need more water?" The royal cupbearer filled Tom's cup again.
Tom needed to do something right now! He beckoned for Lord Hertford to approach the table.
"What's the matter, Your Highness?" Lord Hertford's face was full of concern.
"My nose itches terribly. I have so many servants that there has to be one in charge of my nose. Please summon the royal nose scratcher immediately."
"I'm sorry, sir, but there is no royal nose scratcher," Lord Hertford said.
"No royal nose scratcher?" By now the tears were streaming down Tom's face. "Then what am I supposed to do?"
Lord Hertford was baffled. "Surely this isn't the first time in your life that your nose has itched. What have you done in the past?"
"When I was on Offal . . . " Tom remembered the king's orders. "Oh, I don't care what the proper thing is. I need to scratch my own nose!"
And that's exactly what he did.
No one gasped or laughed. Lord Hertford was just relieved that Tom hadn't said anything more about Offal Street.
"Very good, Your Highness," Lord Hertford said, and the servants broke into applause.

The royal napkin holder arrived with a gold bowl filled with rose water. Over his arm he carried a napkin. Tom was supposed to wash and dry his hands after meals, but he didn't know that. He raised the dish to his lips and solemnly took a drink.
"It doesn't have much flavor." Tom handed the bowl back to the royal napkin holder. "Please make it stronger next time," he said to the head chef.
She started to protest, but Tom stood up, which signaled that lunch was over. Tom announced that he wanted to return to his room.
"I'd like to be left alone for the rest of the afternoon," he said.
As soon as his door closed, Tom began hunting for a nutcracker. "Prince Edward has everything, so he must have a nutcracker."
But before he found one, he was distracted by shelves full of books. One book was about castles and forts. Another was about famous kings and queens of the past.
"Father Andrew would like that," Tom thought. "There are so many books here that I don't know where to start reading!"
Just then he noticed Royal Court Etiquette: A Guide for the Young Prince .
"That would be useful," Tom thought.
He opened the book and turned the pages. The book covered everything from when to wear a crown to who should bow to whom. There was even a whole chapter on table settings.
"Who knew there were so many types of silverware?" Tom pored over the illustrations of dessert spoons, salad forks, and steak knives. "I guess I should stop using my hands to eat."
Tom soon grew bored with this chapter and turned to the section on armor. He took the book over to the prince's armor to compare it.
Made of metal and covered with gold designs, Prince Edward's armor was beautiful to look at. But Tom wanted to do more than look at it. He wanted to try it on.
"Prince Edward and I are the same size, so I know it'll fit me," he thought. "But I don't think I can get into it without help."
Then he noticed the helmet and armor-covered gloves on a table. As Tom picked up a glove, a heavy metal disk fell out.
"Well, that thing isn't mentioned in the book!" Tom watched the disk roll across the floor. "But it'll be perfect for cracking nuts."
Tom left the disk on the floor while he put on the gloves. Then he put on the helmet and found his way to the mirror. It was hard to see through the slits for his eyes.
"Phew! This helmet is much heavier and hotter than I expected," Tom thought. "I need to take it off." He tried to yank off the helmet, but . . .
"Ahh!"
It was stuck on his head!
When we last saw Edward, he had just arrived on Offal Street.
"Help! Help!" Edward cried as Tom's father, John Canty, dragged him home. A few people followed them.
"Are you all right?" a man in black called out to Edward.
"No, I am not all right!" Edward said indignantly. "I am Prince Edward, and this stranger has kidnapped me!"
"Be quiet, you miserable boy!" John threatened Edward with a stick.
Suddenly the man in black reached out to snatch Edward away from John.
"Stop interfering!" John struck the man, who fell to the ground.

Without looking back, John dragged Edward into a house. They climbed the stairs and John pushed Edward into a smelly, crowded room. Tom's mother was cooking over a fire in the fireplace, while his sister, Nancy, hung laundry nearby.
"I found Tom wandering the streets," John said.
"I told you before that I'm not Tom!" Edward stamped his foot. "I'm Prince Edward. Take me back to the palace gate, and my father, the king, will send Tom out to you."

"Oh, my poor boy!" Tom's mother put her hands on Edward's shoulders and studied his face. "All your reading about royalty has made you think you're a prince. But that's not true. Can't you see that I'm your mother?"
Edward shrugged off her hands. "I've never seen you before in my life."
Tom's mother began to cry. "Oh, Tom, what's wrong with you?"
John laughed and ordered Nancy to curtsy to the prince.
"Father, please stop teasing Tom and let him go to bed," Nancy said. "He'll be better in the morning."
"Speaking of the morning . . ." John turned to Edward and held out his hand. "The rent's due tomorrow. Hand over what you earned begging today."
"Begging? Princes don't beg!" Edward was insulted that John was bothering him about money.
John growled. "Go to bed before I lose my temper and hit you!"
Edward looked around the room but didn't see any beds. "Where am I supposed to sleep?"
"Over there in that corner as usual," Nancy said quietly. She pointed to a pile of old blankets and straw.
Edward was too tired to protest. He went over and lay down on the floor.
Later, when everyone was asleep, Tom's mother tiptoed over to Edward.
"I saved you some bread crusts," she said.
Edward sat up and took a bite of stale bread. "Thank you, good woman. The king will reward your kindness."
Tom's mother shook her head sadly and went back to her bed.
"Something's not quite right," she thought. "Maybe this boy isn't Tom. Oh, but that's absurd."
She tried to sleep but kept thinking, "If only there was some way to test him—"
Suddenly Edward made a sound in his sleep as if he'd been startled.
"That's it!" Tom's mother said softly. "Tom always makes an odd gesture whenever he's startled, even in his sleep. He covers his eyes with his palm out."
She crept to Edward's side with a candle and struck the floor with her fist. His eyes flew open, but he didn't make the gesture. She tried twice more with the same result.
"I don't understand. He's made that gesture his whole life." Tom's mother sadly crept away. "Something is wrong with my boy, but I won't give up on him."
Around midnight everyone was awakened by a knock at the door.
Tom's father stopped snoring. "Who's there?" he shouted. "What do you want?"
"I came to warn you," said a voice outside the door. "That man you hit with your stick was Father Andrew. He's badly injured, and you're going to be arrested."
"Get up! We have to leave right now!" John shouted to his family.
Five minutes later the Cantys and Edward were flying down the stairs. They moved quickly through the dark streets. As they neared the bridge, they heard people cheering the prince and the mayor.
"I'm supposed to be at the mayor's banquet!" Edward suddenly remembered.
A line of bonfires stretched up and down both sides of the river. Periodically there was a great booming sound as fireworks filled the sky. People danced and sang in the streets.
The Cantys and Edward joined the crowd.
"If we get separated, we'll meet on the bridge," John shouted to his family.
But Edward had other plans. From the moment they'd left the house, he had been hoping to escape.
Suddenly a man bumped into John, who lost his grip on Edward.
Edward seized the opportunity and ran off. "If I find Tom at City Hall, pretending to be me, he'll spend the rest of his life in prison. I'll make sure of that!"
A few hours before the mayor's banquet, Tom was still struggling to remove the prince's helmet.
"Perhaps I should call for help," he thought. But then he remembered the nuts from lunch. He wanted to eat them without anyone watching him.
Tom took off the armored gloves, hoping that would make it easier to remove the helmet. But the helmet didn't budge.
"Ugh!" he shouted in frustration.
Immediately someone knocked on the door. A servant spoke but did not enter the room. "I know you don't want to be disturbed this afternoon, but do you need any help?"
"No! Go away!" Tom shouted.
He pulled on the helmet, but it was still stuck. Finally he tucked in his chin and gave a mighty tug. The helmet popped off and hit the floor with a crash.
There was another knock at the door.
"Excuse me, sir," the same servant said. "Are you all right?"
"I'm fine!" Tom shouted. In his dreams about being a prince, he had never had to deal with nosy servants!
At last he settled down on the floor with the nuts. The heavy metal disk made a perfect nutcracker. When he finished eating, he put the disk back where he found it—inside an armored glove.

That night Tom was aboard the royal barge with Princess Elizabeth and Lady Jane. As they sailed down the river toward City Hall, he was amazed by the sights and sounds. Bonfires burned on both riverbanks, and fireworks boomed overhead.
"I've never seen anything like this!" Tom blurted out. "And it sounds like people are cheering for the prince. I mean, me!"
Princess Elizabeth and Lady Jane looked at each other.
"This isn't the first time people have cheered for him," Lady Jane whispered. "Why doesn't he know that?"
Princess Elizabeth shrugged. "But remember, we're supposed to act like nothing's wrong with him."
The banquet took place in a special room in City Hall. At the sound of a horn, a servant paraded a large piece of meat around the head table. The mayor and Tom both made toasts.
"Excellent toast, Your Highness," Lord Hertford whispered.
Tom smiled. "That etiquette book has already come in handy," he thought as he sat down to enjoy the meal.

Dinner was followed by entertainment, which continued for hours. Sometime after midnight Tom was busy watching a juggler. At that moment Edward arrived outside City Hall and demanded to be let into the banquet.
"I'm Prince Edward, and this banquet is in my honor!" he said to the guard.
"Well, I'm a guard, and my job is to keep paupers outside. Prince Edward arrived hours ago."
"I knew it!" Edward said. "That imposter has been wearing my clothes all day, and now he thinks he's the real prince!"
Several people gathered around Edward. Amused by his accusations, they were hoping to prod him into saying more outrageous things.
"Go home," the guard said to Edward.
"I can see that I don't have any friends here," Edward said, "but I'm not backing down. When that imposter comes outside, I'll confront him."
A tall, muscular man appeared next to Edward. His clothes were made of expensive fabric that was now faded and worn. A rusty sheath held his sword. He looked almost as poor as Edward did.
"I admire your courage," the man said. "My name is Miles Hendon, and I'll be your friend."
"Judging by this fellow's clothes, he's another prince in disguise!" said a man who was watching the scene. "Let's throw them both in the river!"
But before anyone could grab them, someone arrived on horseback.
"Make way for the king's messenger!" the rider shouted.
Miles took advantage of the opportunity to scoop up Edward and flee.
The messenger strode into the banquet hall and blasted his horn.
"A message from the palace," he announced. "The king is dead!"
The guests bowed their heads. Then they fell to their knees and stretched out their hands toward Tom.
The whole building seemed to shake as they cried, "Long live the king!"
Tom gulped as he took in this astonishing spectacle. For a moment he didn't know what to say, but finally something occurred to him. He told the guests to stand.
"My reign will be one of mercy and peace," Tom said. "As my first official act, I declare that the Duke of Norfolk will not die."
Tom turned to Lord Hertford. "I never understood why my father sentenced him to death."
"Long live King Edward!" The crowd cheered and applauded.
Tom looked out at his loyal subjects and felt his confidence fade. "How long can I keep fooling all these people?" he whispered.
Miles pulled Edward away from City Hall. Heading toward the river, they heard the same news being passed from one person to another.
"Have you heard? The king is dead!"
The words made Edward shudder, and tears came to his eyes. The man who had been such a tyrant to others had always been gentle with him.
"The country has lost a king, but I have lost a father." Edward wiped away a tear with his hand.
Miles patted Edward on the back while encouraging him to hurry.
"Long live the king!" a man shouted as they stepped onto the bridge.
"Long live King Edward!" others shouted.
"That's me!" Edward said. "How strange and wonderful it seems at the same time!"
Miles frowned. "Something is wrong with this boy," he thought. "He believes he's the king."
Miles decided to go along with the pauper's fantasy for now. "Yes, Your Highness."
Edward stopped walking and waited for Miles to stop and turn around.
"Actually, now that I'm king," Edward said, "you should address me as 'Your Majesty' or 'sir.' By the way, where are we going?"

Miles walked back to where Edward was standing. "To an inn on the other side of the bridge. Then after a meal and a good night's sleep, we'll head to Hendon Hall, my family's home in the country. You'll be safe there, Your Majesty."
"I'd prefer to go to the palace and—"
"So," a voice growled suddenly, "you finally decided to show up!" John Canty reached out a hand to seize Edward. "You won't escape again! If you do, I'll—"
Miles stepped between them. "Not so fast, my friend. You don't need to be so hard on the boy. And why are you bothering him anyway?"
"Not that it's any of your business, but he's my son."
"You're lying!" Edward peered around Miles to glare at John. "I hate you, and I'd rather die than go anywhere with you!"
"Then it's settled," Miles said. "The boy stays with me."
"We'll see about that!" John tried to push past Miles to reach Edward.
But Miles raised one arm to block John and put his other hand on his sword.
"Don't even think of touching this lad!" Miles warned. "I just saved him from being thrown in the river. I'm not going to let you do something worse to him!"
For a moment John looked like he might challenge Miles. But then, muttering curses and threats, he moved away.
"Phew! That was close!" Edward said. "That man keeps mistaking me for his son."
"Don't worry, Your Majesty," Miles said as they crossed the bridge. "I vow to protect you from all danger and nurse you back to health. Think of me as your older brother."
"Thank you for your protection, but I'm not sick," Edward said. "And if you were my older brother, you'd be king instead of me."
"I guess that's right," Miles said slowly. "Well, here we are at the inn where I'm staying."
Miles ordered some hot food to be sent to his room on the top floor. Their meal soon arrived.
"We'll have a regular feast." Miles rubbed his hands together in anticipation. "It may not be as fine as the mayor's banquet, but—"
He was stopped by the sight of Edward standing at the wash basin.
"What are you waiting for, lad?"
"I want to wash my hands and face."
"Oh, is that all? You don't need my permission to do that."
Edward remained motionless, except for impatiently tapping his foot.
"What's the problem?" Miles said. "The water and the towel are right there."
"Please stop talking and pour the water into the basin," Edward said.
Trying not to laugh, Miles picked up the pitcher and did as he was told. "My goodness," Miles thought. "He's acting like he really is a member of the royal family."
"Ahem! I need to dry myself." Edward raised an eyebrow, indicating the towel that was right in front of him.
Miles obediently handed him the towel. While Miles washed his own face and hands, Edward sat at the table. Miles pulled out the other chair and prepared to join him.
"What are you doing?" Edward cried. "I'm sitting! And no one else sits while the king is sitting—not without the king's permission. Your role is to serve me."
"Yes, Your Highness. Forgive me." Amused, Miles stood obediently behind Edward's chair.
As Edward ate, he relaxed and became more friendly. "I think you said that your name is Miles Hendon?" Edward put down his fork. "I'd like to know more about you. Please tell me your story."
"I was forced to leave home ten years ago." Miles began his story while Edward continued to eat.
Edward raised his eyebrows in surprise. "Why?"

"I'm from a wealthy noble family," Miles said. "My mother died when I was young. My father, Sir Richard, is a kind man. So is my older brother, Arthur. But my younger brother, Hugh, is evil and plotted against me. We—"
"I don't have any brothers, just one sister," Edward interrupted.

"Yes, Your Majesty." Miles continued the story. "We have a dear friend, Lady Edith, whose family is even wealthier than mine. Her parents are dead, and she has no siblings. So my father is her guardian. Beautiful, wonderful Edith!"
Miles paused and sighed. "I always loved her even though she was engaged to Arthur from an early age. And I know that she loved me."
Edward pointed his fork at Miles. "You're not supposed to be in love with your brother's fiancée. Even I know that."

"Oh, but Arthur didn't care. He was in love with someone else and wanted to break the engagement. He told us to be patient and that everything would work out." Miles sighed again. "Unfortunately, my father wouldn't allow the engagement to be broken. He felt it would reflect badly upon our family."
"So did Edith marry Arthur?"

"No, my brother Hugh declared that he was in love with Edith. But everyone knew he was really in love with her money. The only person he fooled was my father, who always treats Hugh like his favorite son."
Edward remembered how Miles had protected him. "I can't believe you let Hugh get away with that."

"I was a wild young man, but I wasn't a bad person," Miles said. "However, Hugh exaggerated my faults to our father. He bribed a servant to help him hide a rope ladder in my room. Then Hugh told our father that I was planning to elope with Edith."
"But Hugh was lying!" Edward pounded his fist on the table.

"Exactly," Miles said. "My father was furious with me. He made me join the army, thinking three years as a soldier would teach me a lesson. In my last battle, I was captured by the enemy and spent seven years in prison. I recently escaped and am on my way home after ten years."
"That's outrageous!" Edward jumped up from the table. "As your king, I will make things right. Now let me tell you my story."
Edward launched into his tale of switching clothes with Tom.

Miles listened in amazement. "For a pauper, Edward knows a lot about the royal family and the palace," he thought. "Poor child. I'll make sure he gets the care he needs until he's well again. And until then, I'll just go along with whatever he says."
Edward finished his story at the point where he met Miles.
"You saved me from shame and injury, and possibly saved my life and my crown," Edward said. "How can I reward you?"
"I just did what any loyal subject would do," Miles said. "I don't need anything in return."
But Edward insisted on rewarding him.

"Well, there is one thing," Miles said. "Back in history, there was a man who was not required to remove his hat whenever he was with the king. I'd like to have a similar privilege—I'd like to be allowed to sit when you sit."
"A reasonable request," Edward said. "And one that I grant not only to you, but to your heirs. In addition I will make you a knight."
Miles handed Edward his sword and knelt before him. Edward tapped him on each shoulder with the sword.
"Rise, Sir Miles! And sit down!"
"Thank goodness," Miles thought, "Edward is now permitting me to sit. Otherwise, I'd be standing until he was cured of this delusion that he's king!"

By this point both Edward and Miles were exhausted. Edward stood up and went over to Miles' bed. He seemed to assume that it was his place to sleep. Miles had assumed that Edward would sleep on the floor.
"It's time for you to help me get ready for bed." Edward sat on the bed.
Miles helped Edward remove his shoes. "And where am I to sleep?"
"You will lie in front of the door and guard it." Edward lay down and promptly fell asleep.
Miles watched the sleeping child and smiled. "He could have been born into the royal family—he plays the part so naturally. Sleep well, my little king."
Then Miles stretched out on the floor in front of the door and went to sleep too.
The next morning Miles was about to leave when Edward woke up.
"Where are you going?" Edward said in a sleepy voice. "I'm freezing."
"I'm just going out to run an errand," Miles replied. "You'll be warmer if you pull the covers over your head."
Too tired to order Miles to do that for him, Edward just grunted and tugged on the covers.
Half an hour later, Miles returned with some secondhand clothes for Edward. Made of cheap material, they clearly showed signs of wear.
"At least they're clean and warm, and I can mend the smaller holes," Miles thought. "I hope they're the right size."

Miles held up a shirt and compared it to the lump in the bed across the room. He sat down and took out a needle and thread. It took him five tries, but at last he succeeded in threading the needle. Miles hummed quietly while he worked on his mending.
"Ouch! That's a sharp needle!" Miles said aloud. He sucked his finger as he looked over at the bed. Edward did not stir.
"Poor lad must be exhausted," he thought. "I'll have to wake him soon, so we can eat and be on our way to Hendon Hall."
Miles wished he had more money, so that he could afford better clothes for Edward. But these would have to do. He still needed to pay for their food and lodging along the way.
Finished with the mending, Miles called Edward. "Time to get up, Your Majesty!"
There was still no sign of life from the lump in the bed.
Miles finally approached the bed and threw back the covers. "Edward?"
The boy was gone!
Miles looked around the small room. There was no place for Edward to hide. Just then someone knocked at the door. Miles opened it, expecting Edward, but a servant pushed past him with breakfast.
"Not so fast!" Miles said. "Have you seen the boy who was with me?"
The servant laid the dishes on the table. "Um—"
"Where is he?" Miles demanded.

"Soon after you left, a young man came to the inn." The servant anxiously wrung his hands. "He said that you wanted the boy to meet you in the woods beyond the bridge. So I brought the young man to your room. He woke up the lad and delivered his message."
"And what did the boy say to that? I can't imagine he was very happy."

"Well, he did grumble about being disturbed 'so early,' as he put it. But he left with the young man right away. On the way out, he remarked that you showed bad manners in sending a stranger instead of coming yourself."
"I didn't send a stranger, you fool!" Miles began to pace the room. "Perhaps no harm will come to the boy. I'll eat and then I'll go in search of him. Quick! Set the table. No, wait!"
Miles stopped pacing. "Someone tried to make it look like the boy was still in bed. Why?"
"I don't know for sure," the servant said, "but I saw the young man fooling with the covers."
"It's clear that someone wanted to deceive me." Miles smacked his forehead with his hand. "Whoever it was wanted to gain time so they could escape. Was the young man alone?"
"Yes, all alone."
"Are you sure?" Miles persisted. "Think hard."

The servant wrinkled his brow as if that would help him think. "Oh! Now I remember! No one came here with the young man. But I happened to be looking out the window when he and the boy reached the bridge."
"What happened then?" Miles thundered impatiently.
"Just then the innkeeper called me—"
"No, no! What happened to the boy?"
"A man dressed in rags stepped out of the shadows and followed them."
"Did you get a good look at him?"
"His arm was in a sling, and he had a patch over one eye."
Miles sat down at the table and rubbed his eyes. "I can't believe I've lost my poor little friend. I promised myself I'd take care of him until he was well."
"Don't worry. I'm sure you'll find him. And one more thing," the servant said as he opened the door. "That fellow with the eye patch? He limped slightly and walked with a cane."
"Oh no!" Miles groaned. "That man is probably the same brute who claimed that Edward was his son!"
Miles stood up. He hated to leave his food, but he had to find Edward at once. The boy could be in trouble!
That same morning Tom woke up before it was light. He thought he was back in his family's room on Offal Street.
"Hey, Nancy, wake up!" he called softly to his sister. "I just had a dream that I was king! Can you believe it?"
A shadowy form appeared next to Tom's bed in the palace. "Did you call, Your Majesty?"
"Your Majesty?" Tom groaned. "Oh, then it wasn't a dream after all."
Tom fell back to sleep. Soon he was happily dreaming about a pot of gold coins buried next to a tree. In this dream Tom dug up the coins and hurried home to his mother.
"These are all for you, Mother. You'll never be hungry again!" Tom proudly dropped the coins in her lap. "And I didn't steal or beg for any of them!"
Gathering Tom into her arms, his mother said, "It's late, Your Majesty. Are you ready to get up?"
"Ugh!" Tom cried. That was not the answer he was expecting. He opened his eyes and realized once again that he was still king.
"And I'm still a prisoner in this palace," he thought.
"Time to get dressed, sir," the servant said.
When he sat up, Tom noticed more servants standing around his room. "Why are there so many people here?" he asked the first servant.
"To assist Your Majesty with the morning ritual of dressing."
"I can dress myself!" Tom snapped. He heard a sharp intake of breath from one servant and realized he'd made a mistake. "Or . . . you can all help me."
The servants formed a line. Starting near the door, each garment was passed down the line until it reached Tom.
"This is going to take forever," Tom thought.
And it did.
At last there was only one more garment to go—a silk stocking. Slowly it made its way toward Tom. But when the stocking reached the servant closest to Tom, the man held it up.
"Look at that hole! The king can't wear a less than perfect stocking!"

He handed the stocking to the servant behind him, and it slowly returned to the last servant. After some delay a perfect stocking was found and sent down the line to Tom. He put that on along with his shoe.
"I hope this is the end because I'm hungry." Tom stood up and admired himself in the mirror.
"I'm sorry, Your Majesty, but you can't leave your room until the royal hairdresser has styled your hair."
Tom groaned and sat down again. "Bring on the combs and brushes, and let's get this over with!"
After breakfast Tom met with his royal advisers around a large table. Each of them had something for Tom to approve.
Lord Hertford sat at Tom's side, whispering helpful advice as needed. "Sign and date this document . . . Give your consent for that meeting . . . Refuse to approve that expense . . ."
Tom remembered playing with his friends from Offal Street. "Julian and the others were better royal advisers," he thought. "They were much more fun!"
The royal treasurer read an accounting of the expenses for King Henry's household.
"What?" Tom gasped. "That's a lot of money!"
"Yes, Your Majesty." The treasurer showed Tom the number in her account book. "And most of that money is still owed."
"You mean we haven’t been paying our bills?" Tom was horrified. Many people on Offal Street couldn't pay their bills, but he expected the royal family to do so.
The royal treasurer adjusted her glasses. "That's right, sir. The royal bank accounts are almost empty, and the servants haven't been paid."
"We will have to economize at once!" Tom said. "First of all, we should sell this palace and move somewhere less expensive. I know of a little house by the fish market. Perhaps we could move there."

Tom felt a sharp pressure on his arm and knew it was a signal from Lord Hertford. He stopped talking. He remembered his dream about giving his mother the pot of gold coins. Apparently he couldn't do that even as king.
"Maybe I could make my mother a duchess," he thought as a secretary droned on about the late king's will.

But then he looked around the table. These advisers were the ones who kept the kingdom running. If he suggested making his mother the Duchess of Offal Street, they'd think he was ill. And then they'd do nothing.
The dull work went on until Tom's head began to nod and he fell asleep.
Lord Hertford sighed. "We have to stop now," he whispered to the others. "We can't do anything more without the king's signature."
That afternoon Tom was eating nuts in his room. When someone knocked on the door, he quickly hid the nuts and nutcracker in the armored glove.
"Come in!" Tom called, trying to act normally.
Tom was surprised when a thin boy entered the room. He appeared to be about 12 years old. With his head bowed, he dropped to his knees before Tom.
"Rise, lad," Tom said. "Who are you, and what do you want?"
The boy stood and looked at Tom with some concern. He'd heard the rumors about the prince's illness and knew he shouldn't act surprised. But he couldn't help himself.
"Oh, surely you must remember me, Your Majesty. I'm Marlow, your whipping boy."
Tom had no idea what a whipping boy did, so he couldn't pretend to know Marlow.
"Lord Hertford should have told me about him," Tom thought.
But Tom knew that Lord Hertford couldn't be by his side every minute. Something similar was bound to happen again. Tom needed a way to cope by himself, and he decided to practice on this boy.

"My whipping boy . . ." Tom tapped his chin as if he was thinking. "Hmm. I dimly remember you, but my illness has affected my mind. Can you give me a little clue about yourself? That sometimes jogs my memory."
"Do you remember a few days ago when you made three mistakes during your Greek lesson?"
"Maybe . . ." Meanwhile Tom thought he'd probably make forty mistakes if he really was taking Greek.
"Your teacher was going to whip me because you were too lazy to study."
Tom was astonished. "Whip you for something that was my fault?"
"Yes, your teachers always whip me when you fail at your lessons. No one may strike you, so I take your punishments for you," Marlow explained patiently. "That's my job, and I get paid for it."
Tom thought this was a very strange way to earn a living. "And has my Greek teacher beaten you this week as planned?"

"No, Your Majesty. The whipping was scheduled for today but was canceled because we're in mourning for King Henry. So . . ." Marlow hesitated. "So I've taken a chance and come to remind you of your promise. You offered to plead with your teacher on my behalf."
"Ah, now I remember. Yes, I'll talk to him for you."
"Thank you, sir." Marlow paused. "Some people would say you've been kind enough, but I have another favor to ask."
"Go on. I'm feeling in a generous mood." Tom encouraged Marlow to sit down.

"Now that you're king, you can do whatever you want. Which means you can stop having lessons. But if you do that, there will be no need for a whipping boy. I don't like being whipped, but I'll lose my job and my home here." Marlow dropped to his knees again. "Please, sir, don't turn me out on the street!"
Tom liked Marlow and was happy to help.
"Rise, Marlow. From here on, all whippings will be banned in the palace, but you'll have a job for life."
Marlow heaved a sigh of relief. "Oh, thank you, sir! But what will I do?"
"You can answer my questions," Tom said. "You know a lot about what goes on here, and it helps my memory to talk to you. Let's start with . . ."
After an hour Tom had gained valuable information about royal people and events. And Marlow was pleased too. He felt that he had helped the king to get better.
"You've earned your wages today," Tom said. "I want you to visit me every day and update me on what's happening."
Soon after Marlow left Tom's room, Lord Hertford arrived.

"I'm sorry to bring disturbing news, Your Majesty." Lord Hertford took a deep breath. "Your advisers fear that news of your illness has leaked. They want you to start dining regularly in public. Seeing you in good health will reassure people."
An hour ago this news would have surprised Tom. But Marlow had heard gossip about the advisers' plan and passed it on to Tom.
"I can understand why they'd think this was a good idea," Tom said.

Lord Hertford was relieved that the king was acting more like himself. He decided to test Tom with a few questions. Thanks to Marlow, Tom was able to respond intelligently. Encouraged by Tom's replies, Lord Hertford asked one last question.
"Do you remember where you put the Great Seal?"
"No." Tom shook his head. "What does that look like?"
Lord Hertford hid his disappointment. The king was obviously still not well. "It doesn't really matter, Your Highness. Now that King Henry is dead, you'll soon have a new seal of your own."

As the days passed, Tom started getting used to being king. He still wasn't comfortable in the role, and he was sometimes homesick. But he accepted that everyone had to bow to him and that getting dressed was a group project.

Dining in public was supposed to begin on the fourth day of Tom's reign. That morning he had a meeting with his advisers. Lord Hertford was talking about important matters, and Tom should have been listening. But he was in a bad mood because he was dreading lunch.
"Everyone will be watching me and whispering about me," he thought. "What if I make a mistake?"
Tom's thoughts were interrupted by the sound of shouting outside. Eager for any distraction, he jumped up from the table. He ran to the window but couldn't see anything.
"I wonder what's going on," Tom said.
"I'll send a messenger to find out," Lord Hertford said.
A few minutes later, the messenger returned.
"A crowd is following three people—a man plus a woman and her daughter," the messenger said. "They've been sentenced to death."
"To death?" Tom said. "Bring them here. I want to hear what they've done to deserve such an awful punishment."
The three doomed prisoners soon arrived, accompanied by a sheriff. As they knelt before Tom, he studied their faces.
"There's something familiar about that man," Tom thought. "I feel like we've met before, but that's impossible." He asked the sheriff what the man was accused of doing.
The sheriff looked serious as he answered the question. "This criminal poisoned a man to death."
Startled, Tom turned to the man. "Is this true?"
"No, Your Majesty. The evidence against me is very weak."
"I'd like to hear that evidence. Sheriff?"

"Three witnesses say this man—a stranger—entered a house where another man lay sick in bed," the sheriff began. "It was ten o'clock in the morning. The sick man was alone at the time and sleeping. This man soon left the house, and the sick man died within the hour."
"Did anyone see this man give poison to the sick man?" Tom asked. "Was any poison ever found?"
"No, Your Majesty."
Tom scratched his head and looked puzzled. "Then how do you know he was poisoned?"

"The doctors said his symptoms could only be caused by poisoning. And there's more: A while ago a witch told several people that the man would be poisoned. And . . . " The sheriff took a deep breath for dramatic effect. "That a stranger would give the poison!"
Tom was not impressed. "Most of the world is made up of strangers."
"That's true," one of Tom's advisers whispered to Lord Hertford, who nodded in agreement.
"Yes, Your Majesty," the sheriff said. "But the witch said that the stranger would have brown hair and wear plain clothing just like this man."
It was hard for Tom to argue with that.
"What do you have to say for yourself?" Tom asked the man. "Can any of your friends speak on your behalf?"
"No, Your Majesty." The man looked sad. "As you've already heard, I'm a stranger here, so I have no friends. But if I may speak in my own defense . . ."
Tom nodded to grant him permission.
"I'm accused of poisoning a man. But at that exact moment, I wasn't taking a life. In fact I was saving a life! A boy was drowning—"
Tom held up his hand for silence because he suddenly recognized this man.
"He's the one who pulled Julian from the river!" Tom thought. "But I have to be sure."
"On what date is he accused of committing this crime?" Tom asked the sheriff.
"Well, that's easy for me to remember." The sheriff puffed up his chest with pride. "It was New Year's Day!"
"The same day that Julian almost drowned!" Tom thought.
"Let the prisoner go free! It is the king's will!" Tom shouted. "That other man may have been poisoned, but it wasn't by this man."
Tom was momentarily embarrassed by his outburst. But he quickly recovered.
"I'm enraged that a man was sentenced to death based on such ridiculous evidence," Tom went on. "Such gossip shouldn't even be called evidence."
A low buzz of admiration for Tom's intelligence went around the table.
"The king asked such good questions," one adviser said to another.
"I don't see any signs of illness in the boy," the second adviser said.
Lord Hertford rapped on the table to get the advisers' attention. "Now let's resume our discussion of the royal stables. The horses—"
"Just a minute," Tom interrupted. "I want to hear what the other two prisoners have to say!"
"I just saved a man from execution!" Tom thought, feeling proud. Now he wanted to talk to the mother and daughter. They were also sentenced to death.
Looking at the terrified girl clinging to her mother, Tom was filled with compassion. She was his age or possibly even younger. What could she have done to deserve the death sentence?
"Tell me, Sheriff. What are these two accused of?" Tom secretly hoped the sheriff's evidence was as flimsy as in the last case.

"Well, this is quite a strange situation." The sheriff jerked his thumb at the mother and daughter. "These two are accused of using their supernatural powers to create a huge storm. More than forty people have testified about the terrible destruction it caused."
Tom sat back in his chair to think. Clearly this was not the answer he had expected. After a few moments, he asked another question.
"Did this woman also suffer from the storm?"
"Indeed she did, Your Majesty," the sheriff said. "Her house was swept away, and she and her daughter were left homeless."
"It's hard to believe that someone would deliberately cause such damage to her own home," Tom said.
"That's a good point," one of Tom's advisers said to the other.
"The king's very sharp today," the other replied proudly.
By now almost everyone in the room—including Tom—was rooting for the mother and daughter.
"So, Sheriff, perhaps you can tell us how these two caused such a storm?"
"By pulling off their stockings, sir."
This reply was so ridiculous that Tom had to struggle to keep from laughing.
"Really?" Tom bit his lip. "Has removing their stockings always had this effect?"
"Always, if the woman utters the right words."
Tom turned to the woman and issued a command.
"Use your powers! I want to see a storm!"

All of Tom's advisers—including Lord Hertford—turned pale. They squirmed in their seats and looked as if they wanted to flee the room. But Tom was so eager to see the woman's magical powers that he didn't notice.
The woman looked puzzled.
"Don't worry," Tom said. "You won't be accused of anything. Moreover I decree that you'll both go free, and no one will be able to harm you. Go ahead, use your powers to make a storm for me."
"Oh, Your Majesty," the woman said softly. "I don't have any such powers."

"I understand," Tom said sympathetically. "Your fears are holding you back. Let me reassure you that I mean what I say. I don't need a big storm. In fact, I'd prefer one that doesn't do much harm because I don't want anyone to get hurt. But make me a storm—even a small one—and you and your daughter will go free."
The woman began to cry, and her daughter whimpered.
"If I could produce such a miracle," the woman said, "I'd gladly do it to save my child's life. Even if you still sentenced me to death. But I have no idea how to make a storm."
Tom thought that sounded like something his mother would say. She would be willing to sacrifice her own life for her child's too.

"Someone give this woman a handkerchief!" Tom commanded. Then he addressed the woman again. "I think you're telling the truth. You and your daughter are free to go on one condition. That you both take off your stockings. If you manage to produce a storm, I'll make you rich."
"Oh, thank you, kind sir!"
The woman immediately kicked off her shoes and started to remove her stockings. Her daughter did the same. While Tom eagerly awaited the coming storm, his advisers tried to hide their anxiety.
"Are you sure this is a good idea, Your Majesty?" Lord Hertford asked.
Tom raised his hand to silence his chief adviser. "And if you can make it snow," he said to the woman, "I'll double your reward."
The girl smiled at the mention of snow.
"Look, Your Majesty, a storm is coming!" The sheriff pointed out the window. "A cloud is covering the sun!"

Tom stood up and went over to the window. He looked from the cloud to the woman to the cloud again. "I see that cloud, but—yes, that's what I thought—it's just a cloud and not a storm. The sun is coming out again."
Everyone but the sheriff sighed with relief, and the woman hurried her child toward the door.
"If your powers ever return," Tom called out, "promise me that you'll come back and make a storm for me!"
"Oh yes, Your Majesty, of course!" the woman said.
Tom grinned while all his advisers shuddered with horror.

"Your Majesty, I'm impressed that you saved those people." Lord Hertford gathered up his papers from the advisers' meeting. "You showed real persistence in dealing with that sheriff. I heard many comments about how dignified and royal you appeared."
"After questioning the sheriff and freeing those people, I feel more like a king," Tom said. "But I'm still a little nervous about dining in public today."
"Oh, I'm confident you'll do well at that—and at your coronation next month."
"My coronation?"

Tom hadn't thought about a coronation, but of course there would be one. A king wasn't really a king until he received his crown in a long, boring ceremony. Father Andrew's books were full of coronations. Tom's stomach rumbled. Was that panic or was he just hungry?
Tom gave Lord Hertford a weak smile. "Is it all right to postpone thinking about my coronation until after lunch?"
Lord Hertford nodded. "Perfectly fine, Your Majesty."
Tom straightened up so that he stood as tall as possible. "Then let's go!"

That afternoon Tom felt remarkably calm in the palace's magnificent banquet hall. A trumpeter sounded a horn as Tom took his seat. His table was on a raised platform so that everyone could watch him eat.
Tom looked down at the people eager for him to begin eating. The whole purpose of this meal was to reassure everyone that he was in good health.
"Now what am I supposed to do?" Tom thought. He closed his eyes, trying to recall his instructions from Lord Hertford. "Oh yes, now I remember."

He nodded to his advisers and other people that he recognized. He allowed the royal napkin holder to tie a napkin around his neck. He waited patiently while the royal cupbearer filled his cup with water.
Tom studied the forks, knives, and spoons while the royal taster performed his job.
"There's a lot of silverware on this table," Tom thought. "I hope I remember which piece to use when."
But then he thought of the rule he'd read in the royal etiquette book.
"Always begin with the utensil farthest away from the plate." Tom smiled to himself and picked up the salad fork.

Throughout the meal Tom was careful not to hurry. He didn't do anything for himself that a servant could do for him. As he started to reach for the butter, he stopped and looked at a servant. The man scurried to Tom's side and placed some butter on Tom's baked potato.
"Is that enough butter, Your Majesty?" the servant asked.
Tom nodded.
"Would you like some pepper?" The servant held a huge pepper mill over Tom's plate.
Tom nodded again and thought about the days when he used to play at being a prince.
"We never used to pretend we were having banquets," he thought. "It's hard to think about food when you're hungry."
Tom's mouth watered while the servant cut up his meat and poured gravy over it.
"I could have done that faster myself!" Tom thought as he quickly reached for a piece with the correct fork.
Suddenly the meat slipped from the fork, hit Tom's lap, and bounced onto the floor.
"Ohh!" Everyone in the room groaned and exchanged looks of dismay.
Lord Hertford silently hoped that Tom would leave the meat alone.
"Don't worry, I've got it!" Tom started to reach under the table before he remembered that kings shouldn't do that. "Just joking!"
Everyone laughed, and Lord Hertford sighed with relief. The servant crawled under the table to remove the piece of meat. The royal napkin holder brought Tom a fresh napkin.
"Nancy and I were so hungry, we would have fought over that meat," Tom thought. "I hope someone gets to eat it."
The rest of the meal went perfectly. Tom even dared to ask for a third piece of chocolate cake. He washed his hands in rose water and wasn't even tempted to drink from the gold bowl.
"That wasn't so hard," Tom thought as he stood up. And then he realized he had to burp.
"Oh no!" he thought. "Is it rude for a king to burp in public? If only I had someone to do that for me!"

By this point, Tom could hardly breathe, for fear he would make another mistake. He caught sight of Marlow, standing at the back of the room. Marlow gave him an encouraging smile, and Tom remembered their first conversation.
"Now that you're king," Marlow had said, "you can do whatever you want."
Tom opened his mouth and out came a tremendous blast of sound. He laughed as the noise from the trumpeter's horn covered his burp.
Meanwhile, what happened to Edward during Tom's first days as king? Where did he go when he disappeared?

Edward left the inn with the young man who'd brought the message he said was from Miles. As they walked toward the bridge and the woods, the man with the eye patch followed them. But he was careful to keep out of Edward's sight.
After a few minutes of walking in the woods, Edward sat down on a tree stump and refused to move.
"If Miles wants to talk, he should come to me !" Edward picked up a stone and gave it an angry toss.
The young man looked surprised. "You want to sit here and wait while your friend lies wounded?"
"Wounded? You didn't mention that Miles was wounded!" Edward's attitude instantly changed, and he hopped up. "We must hurry to him!"
"Not so fast." The young man, whose name was Frank, studied the bare trees around them.
"What are you looking for?" Edward said impatiently. "We have to get going!"
"Aha! There's one!" Frank pointed to a small rag tied to a branch. "We need to follow the markers to the old farm."
After a while they came to a clearing with a burned-out house and a ruined barn. Frank stopped outside the barn.
"Miles! Where are you?" Edward called, but no one answered. He looked around in confusion. "Something's not right here."
Frank burst into laughter as the man with the eye patch joined them.
"It was almost too easy to trick him," Frank said to the man.
"Who are you?" Edward asked the man.
"Stop pretending that you don't recognize your own father." John Canty removed his eye patch.
"You aren't my father," Edward said. "My father is dead, and I'm King Edward!"

"It's clear that something's wrong with your mind. I hate to punish you, but if you provoke me, I will." John shook his fist at Edward. "Now, where are your mother and sister? They didn't come to our meeting place on the bridge."
"They're at the palace, of course," Edward said.
John groaned in frustration. While John and Frank talked, Edward wandered into the barn. Lying down on a pile of straw, he thought of his dead father and wept. He was soon asleep.

When Edward woke up, it was dark, and a campfire was burning outside the barn. Gathered around the fire was a small group of people. A man tossed away his crutches, laughing about pretending to be lame. Another man emptied a woman's purse and handed the contents to the group's leader.
"It's a gang of beggars and thieves!" Edward thought as he watched from inside the barn. "They're outlaws!"
"So, John Canty, what brings you back to your old friends?" the leader asked.
"Well, Ruffler, I made the mistake of injuring a priest, and now the law is after me," John said. "I had to flee the city, or they'd throw me in jail."
"You don't want to go to jail," said the man who'd tossed away the crutches. "I ended up in jail after the king seized my farm to graze his sheep."
The group nodded in agreement as the man continued his story.

"My wife died, and I don't know where my children are—or if they're even alive." The man struggled to control his emotions. "I was sent to jail for stealing food, but I escaped. If I'm caught, I'll be hanged."
Edward strode out of the barn. "You will not be hanged, and your land will be returned! As of today, the cruel reign of my father is over."
There was a murmur of surprise among the group.
"And who are you?" Ruffler asked.
"I am King Edward!"
A wild burst of laughter met that announcement.
Edward was outraged. "Is this how you greet your king?"
"Pay no attention to my son," John said. "He's suffering from a strange illness."
But it was too late. Some men grabbed Edward and set him on a barrel for a throne. They crowned him with a tin basin and gave him a ragged blanket for a robe.
"Long live the king!" the group shouted as they mocked Edward.

As for Miles, he frantically searched all day for Edward but couldn't find the boy. Toward evening he gave up and went to an inn. Eating his supper, Miles thought some more about where Edward might be.
"Edward didn't like the house on Offal Street, so he wouldn't return there. He's probably headed for my family's home because that's where we were supposed to go."
The next morning Miles started for Hendon Hall, hoping to find Edward along the way.

Early the next morning, the gang left the hideout in the woods. About noon they reached a village, where they separated because everyone had their own criminal activities to pursue. Ruffler put Frank in charge of Edward.
Frank pulled Edward by the arm. "Come on, we've got work to do."
"You have no right to touch the king." Edward tried to shake off Frank's hand, but the young man held on tightly.
"Just making sure you don't try to run back to your . . . er . . . palace ." Frank flashed an evil grin.
They walked up and down the streets, occasionally stopping to look in shop windows.
"What are you looking for?" Edward said.
"Something to steal."
"Something to steal? Oh no, I'm not helping you steal. It's wrong to—"
"Don't worry, crybaby," Frank snapped. "There's nothing worth stealing in this place. So we're going to beg."
" We ?" Edward was outraged at the suggestion that a king would beg. "You can beg, but I won't do it."
Frank eyed Edward with surprise. "Since when have you reformed?"
"What are you talking about?" Edward asked.
"According to your father, you've spent your whole life begging on the streets of the city."
"John Canty is not my father, and I've never begged a day in my life."
"Listen to me." Frank was angry now. "Since you're too good to beg or steal, you'll play decoy while I beg. Got it?"
Edward was about to argue again when Frank hushed him.
"Here comes a man with a kind face. First I'll pretend I'm sick, and then you call out to him."
Edward gritted his teeth. "There's no way I'm taking part in your scheme."

Frank pinched Edward's arm and snarled in his ear. "You say, 'Oh, kind sir, my poor brother is afflicted with a terrible illness, and we don't know anyone here. Please help us with just one penny from your great riches.' Understand?"
Before Edward could refuse, Frank dropped to the ground in front of the man.
"Oh dear, oh dear!" the stranger cried. "What's wrong? Let me help you!"
"I don't want to trouble you with my illness," Frank said. "My brother will tell you that I'm often sick and racked with pain. All I ask is a penny for food, and then leave me to my misery."
"A penny? I'll give you three pennies!" The man fumbled in his pocket and handed the coins to Frank. "Now come here, lad, and help me carry your brother to the house—"
"I'm not his brother," Edward interrupted.
"Oh, he denies knowing his own brother." Frank groaned as the man bent over him. "We are both sick. While my illness destroys my body, his sickness eats away his mind."
The stranger looked suspiciously from Edward to Frank and back again. "If he's not your brother," the man said to Edward, "then who is he?"
"A beggar and a thief. While you've been giving him pennies, he's been picking your pocket!"
The man's eyes widened in surprise, and he patted his empty pocket. Frank jumped up and ran away with the man in hot pursuit. Without wasting a second, Edward fled in the opposite direction.
