"Expecting the king to beg and steal. Ridiculous!" Edward kept looking back for Frank as he hurried along.
However, as the hours passed and he grew hungry, Edward realized that he'd have to beg for food. He knocked on a farmhouse door, but the owner took one look at his ragged clothes and shooed him away.
"I can manage on my own! I don't need anybody's charity!" Edward shouted as he walked down the farmhouse lane. A cow raised its head and stared after him.
Night arrived with a damp chill. Edward was tired, but every time he sat down to rest, the cold penetrated his bones.
"I have to find somewhere warm to spend the night." He got up and started walking again.

At last he came to a barn, where a farmworker was finishing some chores. Edward waited outside, near the open door. By the light of the man's lantern, he spotted an empty stall and some horse blankets.
"There's my bed!" Edward thought.
As soon as the man left, Edward crept into the dark barn. He put one blanket on the ground, lay down, and pulled the other blanket over him.
"Ugh! These blankets stink of horse, but they'll have to do."
Edward was almost asleep when something touched his face. He sat up in alarm.
"Who's there?" he whispered.
No one replied. Edward lay down with his eyes wide open even though it was too dark to see.
The thing reached out and touched him again!
Edward's heart pounded as he sat up and looked around the stall. He couldn't see what had touched him in the dark.
"Who's there?" Edward called out nervously, but again no one answered.
"Whoever you are, reveal yourself. And if you're a ghost, well . . . I'm not afraid of ghosts!"
Edward sounded much braver than he felt. He wished that the mysterious creature would go away and leave him alone. But it startled him again, this time by slapping his arm.
"Stop that!" Edward cried out.
There was only one thing to do: touch the creature before it touched him again. Edward reached out a trembling hand and touched a long, warm tail.
"You're not a ghost!" Edward laughed with relief. "You're just a calf! Lie down beside me, and we'll keep each other warm."
With his new friend nearby, Edward felt less lonely. As he fell asleep, he thought about how relieved he was to be free of John and Frank.

The next morning Edward was leaving the stall when he heard someone humming. Before he could hide, a little girl carrying a basket entered the barn. Her eyes widened with surprise when she spotted Edward.
"You don't belong here," she said. "Who are you?"
"I'm Edward, your king. Who are you?"
"My name is Priscilla Grant, and I'm honored to meet you, Your Majesty." Priscilla put down her basket and curtsied to Edward.
Edward was surprised at this mark of respect. People usually mocked him when he announced he was king.
"What are you doing in our barn?" Priscilla asked. "We have cows and horses sleeping here, but you're our first king."
Edward told Priscilla everything that had happened since he left the palace.
"I can't remember the last time I had a good meal," he said.
"We don't have much, but my mother always feeds beggars," Priscilla said. "Come with me."
As he followed Priscilla to the farmhouse, Edward made a silent vow. "After I'm crowned, I'll always be kind to children because Priscilla helped me."
Mrs. Grant was surprised to have a king in her kitchen, but she welcomed Edward.
"I pity the boy," she thought as she listened to his story. "There's something wrong with his mind. I'll find out where he belongs and send him home."
Mrs. Grant gave Edward a large chunk of bread and told him to sit by the fire. "That's all I have right now, but lunch will be ready at noon."
She watched the boy for a moment, wondering if he lived outside. Perhaps he was a shepherd.
"So, Priscilla found you in our barn." Mrs. Grant stirred some soup. "Do you have much experience with animals?"
"No, not really." Edward swallowed some bread. "We have dogs and horses at the palace, but the servants take care of them."

At the mention of servants, Mrs. Grant had another idea. Maybe he was a servant. She talked about carrying firewood, scrubbing floors, and polishing boots. But Edward didn't have anything to say about those things.
Mrs. Grant moved on to breaking eggs.
"You should see our head chef break eggs for chocolate cake!" Edward said enthusiastically. "She never drops any shells in the batter. And she makes the best pies and . . ."

Mrs. Grant smiled as Edward described his favorite desserts. "He's eaten a lot of fancy foods," she thought. "He must be a kitchen helper, maybe even in the palace. I'll test him by having him wash dishes."
"Dishes? You want me to wash dishes?" At first Edward was insulted, but then he remembered the family's kindness to him. Washing dishes might be a way to thank them.

After Edward finished the dishes—he broke a cup and a plate—Mrs. Grant had more chores for him. That morning he learned to peel apples, sharpen knives, and sweep the kitchen floor. He didn't do a great job with any of these chores, but Mrs. Grant still gave him lunch.
After lunch Edward was eager to be on his way. However, Mrs. Grant had other ideas and handed him a pail full of kitchen scraps.
"Oh, I don't need more food." Edward tried to hand the pail back to her. "I'm full from lunch."
Mrs. Grant struggled to hide a smile. "These are for the pigs, Your Majesty. Let's go outside, and I'll show you where the pigpen is."
"You've been very kind to me," Edward said as they went outside.
He was about to say that kings don't feed pigs. But just then he spotted two people coming up the front path—John and Frank!
"Thank you for everything. I must be going!" Edward dropped the bucket of scraps. "Right now!"
Edward ran as fast as possible from the farm. He didn't dare look back until he reached the nearby woods.
"Phew! That was close!"

Edward was panting, but he had to keep moving. After a while he stopped to listen for footsteps behind him. But he heard only birds singing in the bare branches above his head. He shivered as a cold breeze hit his sweat-soaked rags.
"I have to find a safe place to hide." Edward ran on and on, frantically searching for a cave, an abandoned house, anything.
As gloom settled over the woods, Edward realized that night was coming. By now it was too dark to see, and he tripped over roots. A vine brushed his face, and he fell into a briar patch.
At last Edward spotted a light coming from a hut. He cautiously peered through a window and spotted a man with long, white hair. Edward decided the man was harmless despite the ax on the wall.
"He's probably a woodsman who likes living alone," Edward thought.
He knocked on the door, and the man called out, "Who's there?"
"King Edward!"
The woodsman opened the door and studied Edward's rags.
"I've turned away many people," he said. "But I welcome a king who has given up the splendors of royalty. You will live here in peace forever."
"Actually . . ." Edward looked around the simply furnished room that smelled of wood smoke and mold. "I was just seeking shelter for tonight."
"We'll see about that." The woodsman beckoned for Edward to sit by the fire.
"I suppose you're wondering why I'm here," Edward said.
"Not really." And with that, the man launched into a rambling tale about himself. Edward felt more uneasy by the minute.
"I might have been safer with John and Frank!" Edward thought.
Finally the woodsman stopped talking and prepared a supper of bread and cheese.
Edward relaxed, thinking, "This won't be so bad."
That night the old man came into the room where Edward was falling asleep.
"If you're King Edward," he said, "then King Henry must be dead."
"Yes," Edward replied in a sleepy voice.
"I only live like this because King Henry stole my house and my land." The woodsman waited for Edward to reply, but he was already asleep.
The woodsman went into the other room and studied the fire. He took his ax off the wall and felt the blade.
"Needs sharpening," he muttered, and went to work.
After midnight he crept into Edward's room. Without a word, he bound and gagged the boy.
The next morning Edward woke up with the woodsman standing over him. He struggled against the ropes that bound his hands and feet.
"Not so fast," the woodsman said. "You're not going anywhere until you apologize for your father's cruelty."
"Mmff!" The gag prevented Edward from talking. His eyes were wild with fear, and his heart was pounding.

Suddenly there was the sound of voices outside the hut. The woodsman threw a blanket over Edward and left the room. Edward could hear men fighting and running away. Then there was a loud knock at the door to the hut.
"Open this door immediately!"
"It's Miles!" Edward thought, filled with relief.
"Where's the boy?" Miles demanded.
"What boy?" the woodsman asked.
"You know who I mean. King Edward! I caught the scoundrels who kidnapped him, and they confessed they'd tracked him to your door."
"Come on, Miles!" Edward thought. "Stop talking and rescue me!"
"You mean that ragged boy who showed up last night?" the woodsman said innocently. "I sent him on an errand."
"An errand? Wait! What's that noise?"
While the two men talked, Edward had been moaning, trying to attract Miles' attention.
"That sound is just the wind in the trees," the woodsman said. "Come outside and I'll show you."
Edward groaned in despair as he heard the door shut. But his spirits improved when the men came back inside a few minutes later.
"I can't wait any longer," Miles said. "I have to leave. Edward must have lost his way in the woods."
"Don't go alone. Let me help you search for him."
As the door closed, Edward lost all hope. "That old man will get rid of Miles and come back to harm me!"
He soon heard the door open again. Edward hoped it was Miles, but he was afraid to look. Instead John and Frank entered the room.
"You're not who I expected!" Edward said, but he was still happy when they freed him.
Without a word, his old enemies grabbed him by the wrists and hurried him out the door.
Edward struggled to free himself from John and Frank. But they tightened their grips on his wrists and dragged him through the woods.
"Let me go!" Edward cried.
"Not after all the trouble we had finding you, my boy." John pinched Edward's arm with his other hand.
"Ow!" Edward tried to kick Tom's father but missed.
"In case you forgot, Ruffler put me in charge of you," Frank said. "He wasn't happy to hear you'd run off. From now on, you'll do what I say!"
Edward didn't reply because he was busy plotting his escape. When they came upon another farmhouse, he hoped this was his opportunity. But Frank had other ideas.
"Here's your chance to be useful," Frank said. "Knock on the door, and if someone answers, beg for money or food. If no one's there, go into the kitchen and steal whatever you can."
Edward grumbled as Frank shoved him toward the house.
"And don't try any tricks!" Frank called out.
Frank and John watched Edward knock on the door. When no one answered, he went inside.
"He's not much of a beggar," John said. "And I need to work with him on stealing, but—"
"Quiet!" Frank held up his hand. "What's he shouting about?"
"Help! Is anybody home?" Edward cried. "I'm King Edward, and I've been kidnapped!"
Frank and John ran for the house and dragged Edward outside.
"That's exactly what I meant by tricks!" Frank snarled.
"Next time I'll plan my escape more carefully," Edward thought. "And next time I'll succeed!"
That night at the gang's campsite, Frank stepped on Edward's toes. Edward knew he'd done it on purpose. The third time it happened, Edward confronted Frank.
"Stay away from my feet, you clumsy oaf!"
Edward showered Frank with insults in English, Latin, and Greek. Everyone gathered around the two of them, clapping and cheering.
"Hooray for the king!" they shouted.
Two men lifted Edward onto their shoulders and paraded him around the camp.
"Your son has quite a vocabulary," Ruffler said to John.
"I taught him everything I know," John said modestly. "But I think he picked up a few words from books."
Frank scowled as he watched everyone congratulating Edward. "I hope that boy is enjoying this," he thought, "because it's the last time he'll humiliate me!"
The next afternoon the gang of beggars and thieves arrived at another village.
"Don't come back empty-handed," Ruffler said to Edward. "And remember to obey Frank at all times."
Frank walked up and down the streets with Edward.
"Getting arrested might teach our young king a lesson," Frank thought. "But the others in the gang like him. So I can't be too obvious about my role in setting him up."
While Frank was plotting his revenge, Edward was looking for a chance to escape. He thought about running when Frank bent over to pick up a penny on the street.
"Not yet," Edward cautioned himself. "I have to wait for just the right moment."
A few minutes later, they saw a woman carrying a fat package in a basket.
"Stay here, and don't move until I come back," Frank said.
"This is it!" Edward thought.
But before Edward could run, Frank sneaked behind the woman and stole her package. He thrust it into Edward's hands.
"Don't follow me!" Frank shouted to Edward as he ran away. "We'll meet up later."
"No!" Edward threw the package on the ground, where it opened to reveal a ham. "I am not a thief!"
"Oh yes, you are!" The woman grabbed Edward and shouted for help.
Meanwhile Frank ran down an alley, from which he gleefully watched Edward's troubles unfold.
"He'll soon be under arrest, and I'll be rid of him for good." Frank laughed as a blacksmith stepped out of his shop to help the woman.
"What's the matter, ma'am?" The blacksmith picked up the ham and put it into the woman's basket.
"I was walking home when this boy stole the ham right out of my basket!"
"I am your king, not a thief." Edward pointed in the direction Frank had fled. "Quick! Go after Frank. He's the one who stole your ham!"
"I'd better get out of here before the little traitor leads them to me." Frank smiled at the thought of Edward in jail. "Now I just have to think of something to tell Ruffler."
Meanwhile Edward continued to struggle in the woman's grasp. "Let go of me!"
"Be quiet!" The blacksmith reached out a strong arm for Edward. "I'm about to teach you a lesson!"
"You'll do nothing of the kind!" A man suddenly grabbed the blacksmith.
Edward's rescuer was Miles.
"This is a matter for the law to take care of." Miles held onto the blacksmith's arm until he released Edward. "Not you."
The blacksmith rubbed his arm as Edward leaped to Miles' side.
"I appreciate your rescuing me," Edward said. "But you took your time getting here, Sir Miles."
"Sir Miles! I forgot that Edward made me a knight." Miles smiled to himself. "He's such a brave, spirited boy. I'm honored to be a knight—even if his kingdom is only an imaginary one."
Miles' thoughts were interrupted by the arrival of the sheriff.
"This must be the boy who stole the ham." The sheriff took out his handcuffs.
"Don't handcuff him!" Miles said. "He'll go quietly to see the judge."
But Edward was outraged and refused to move. "The king does not go to court!"
"You can't expect your subjects to obey the law, if you won't," Miles said.
"Hmm," Edward said. "You may be right. This will give me a chance to see how criminals are treated."
Inside the courtroom the woman told her story to the judge. He quickly convicted Edward of theft. Miles gasped, but Edward stayed calm.
"The poor boy doesn't realize he'll go to jail," Miles thought.
"How much is this ham worth?" the judge asked the woman.
"Five dollars," she said.
The judge frowned. "Perhaps you'd like to think again. He's an ignorant lad, who was probably driven to steal by hunger."
The woman folded her arms across her chest. "No, that's what the ham is worth, and he needs to be taught a lesson."
The judge shifted in his seat. "You do know that the punishment for stealing anything over three dollars is life in prison?"
Wide-eyed with fear, Edward looked at Miles, but Miles was too startled to comfort him.
"Oh, what have I done?" the woman cried. "I don't want the boy to spend his life in prison!"
"I haven't officially recorded the ham's value," the judge said. "There's still time for you to change it."
"Oh, yes! Now that I think again, it's worth only a dollar at most."
"That's better." The judge smiled.
Miles hugged Edward, who let the big man embrace him. But when the judge sentenced him to five days in jail, Edward started to protest.
"Hush!" Miles whispered as the judge stood up to leave. "Don't make the judge change his mind."
"I didn't steal anything, so I shouldn't have to go to prison." Edward stamped his foot.
Miles nodded but was busy watching the sheriff approach the woman. "I wonder what that fellow is up to."
Miles walked over to where the sheriff and the woman were talking.
"That's a fine ham," the sheriff said. "I'll buy it from you for a dollar."
The woman was insulted by his offer. "I only said it was worth a dollar to spare the boy from life in prison. I paid five dollars for it."
"So, you lied when you said it was worth a dollar!" the sheriff said triumphantly. "I guess the boy will spend the rest of his life in prison after all."
"No, no!" The woman shook her head in confusion.
Miles realized that the sheriff was trying to trick her, but he didn't say anything. After watching the woman sell the ham for a dollar, he returned to Edward's side.
"I refuse to go to jail even for only five days." Edward stubbornly crossed his arms.
"Don't worry, I have a plan," Miles said. "Just trust me, and we'll soon be on our way to my family's home."
Having quickly hidden the ham, the sheriff was ready to escort Edward to jail.
"Sheriff, we need to talk." Miles put his arm around the man's shoulders. "Perhaps you could look the other way while this boy escapes."
"But I'd be committing a crime!" the sheriff said. "I should arrest you for even suggesting that!"
"Or perhaps you'll be arrested." Miles paused. "I heard you trick the woman into selling you her ham. Do you want me to tell the judge about that?"
"Oh, I was just joking with her!" The sheriff laughed nervously.
"Really?" Miles said loudly. "You do know the penalty for breaking that law is death?"
"What law?" The sheriff looked frightened.
"The one against paying too little for big pieces of meat. You'd better return that ham to the woman and let Edward go."
"Of course! Right away!" The sheriff hurried off. "I'll tell the judge that the boy simply disappeared."
"Thank you!" Miles said.
"How did you know about that law?" Edward asked as they left the courtroom.
Miles smiled. "I made it up!"
After three days of traveling, Miles and Edward reached Hendon Hall.
"Welcome to Hendon Hall, my king," Miles said as they entered his old home. "There are seventy rooms and thirty servants here. Can you imagine that?"
Edward thought of his palace with its hundreds of rooms and servants. "Actually, I can."

"I've been away for ten years," Miles went on. "But I'm sure my father, my brother Arthur, and Lady Edith will be overjoyed at my arrival. Don't be offended if they ignore you in their excitement at seeing me. They'll soon welcome you into their home and their hearts."
"And what about your other brother?" Edward asked. "The one who lied and said you were eloping with Lady Edith?"
"Perhaps Hugh will be polite to us," Miles said quietly. "That's the best I can hope for."
They entered a spacious room, where a man was writing letters at a table by the fireplace.
"Sit there." Miles pointed Edward toward a chair and rushed over to the man.
"Hello, Hugh, I'm back!" Miles said, smiling broadly.
Edward was surprised that this man was Hugh. "Miles must be so happy to be home that he's even glad to see Hugh," Edward thought.
Hugh shrank back from Miles. Slowly his stare changed from fear to curiosity to pity.
"From the state of your clothes, poor stranger, the world has treated you harshly," Hugh said. "I have no idea who you are, and you've obviously mistaken me for someone else."
Miles shook his head in disbelief. "Are you saying that you don't recognize me, your own brother? Miles Hendon?"
"Can you really be my lost brother?" Hugh's face lit up with surprise. "Let me get a good look at you."
Hugh pulled Miles toward a window. Then Hugh looked Miles up and down, turned him this way and that, and studied him thoroughly.
Meanwhile Miles laughed and chattered on. "Yes, it's your dear old Miles. Oh, this is a great day! Give me your hand, Hugh! Let me kiss your cheek!"
Miles was about to hug his brother, but Hugh raised a hand in protest. "I can't bear this disappointment."
Stunned, Miles couldn't speak for a moment. "What disappointment?"
Hugh shook his head sadly. "Perhaps others will notice something that I've missed, but I'm afraid the letter was correct."
"What letter?"
"A few years ago, we received a letter that Miles had died in battle."
"Well, that's obviously not true!" Miles said angrily. "Call our father! He'll recognize me at once."
"I can't summon the dead," Hugh said.
"Our father is dead? Oh, this is terrible news indeed." Miles' voice trembled as he struggled to control himself. "Then let me see our brother, Arthur."
"Arthur has also died."
"Both of them gone! They were such good people." Miles stopped to wipe tears from his eyes. "Please don't tell me that Lady Edith has died too."
"No, she still lives here," Hugh said.
Miles heaved a sigh of relief. "Then bring her to me—and bring the old servants too."
To Edward's surprise, Hugh nodded.
"Only Margaret and David still work here," Hugh said, "but I'll get them."
After Hugh left the room, Miles went over to Edward. "It's terrible when no one believes you're the person that you say you are."
"I don't doubt that you are Miles Hendon," Edward said. "Do you doubt that I'm the king?"

"Uh . . . um . . ." Miles was saved from replying by Hugh's return. The servants were with him, and a beautiful, sad woman walked slowly behind them. Her eyes were focused on the floor, and she was as pale as a ghost.
Miles sprang toward her. "Oh, my darling Edith!"
At the sound of Miles' voice, Edith blushed. Hugh waved Miles away and said to her, "Do you know him?"
Trembling, Edith raised her head and looked into Miles' eyes. "I've never seen him before." With a moan and a stifled sob, she fled the room.
"Edith!" Miles cried after her.
Hugh grinned and asked the servants if they recognized Miles, but they shook their heads.
"Well, the servants don't know you," Hugh said after he dismissed them. "And neither does my wife."
"Your wife!" In an instant Miles was pinning Hugh to the wall. "I know what happened! You wrote that letter yourself, and then you stole the woman I love and everything that's mine."
Hugh wiggled free from Miles' grasp and ran from the room.
Edward jumped up. "This isn't exactly the welcome you were expecting. Should we leave?"
Miles scowled. "Since my father and older brother are dead, I'm the rightful owner of Hendon Hall." He planted his feet firmly on the floor. "And I'm not going anywhere!"
Edward watched as Miles paced the room in frustration. Several times Miles stopped and banged his fist on the table.
"I really don't understand," Edward said. "It's very strange."
"There's nothing strange about it at all." Miles hit the table again and shouted, "Hugh has been evil since he was a child!"
"No, I was talking about myself," Edward said. "The countryside should be filled with people looking for me. I don't understand why no one has noticed that the king is missing."
Once again Edward wondered if Tom was pretending to be the king. Was that why no one was searching for him?
"I'm sorry," Miles said. "I was so busy with my own troubles that I forgot about yours."
"Well, I have an idea. I'll write a letter in three languages—Latin, Greek, and English—and you'll take it to my chief adviser. After Lord Hertford reads the letter, he'll send for me right away."
"It might be better to wait until I've sorted things out here," Miles said. "Then I'll be in a better position to—"
Now it was Edward's turn to bang his fist on the table and shout. "Your concerns are trivial compared to the fate of my kingdom!"
Then Edward spoke in a gentle voice, as if to apologize. "Don't worry. After I'm crowned, I'll make things right for you."
While Edward sat at the table and wrote his letter, Miles thought about Edith.
"She must have recognized me," he thought. "But she said that she didn't, and Edith would never lie."
Edward finished his letter and handed it to Miles. "Take this straight to the palace first thing tomorrow."

Distracted by his own problems, Miles stuck the letter in his pocket. Just then the door opened, and Edith entered the room. Her face was still pale and sad, but she held her head up as she approached Miles.
He stepped forward eagerly to meet her. "Edith, my darling! I knew you recognized me, and now you've come back—"
"Please stop talking and sit down," Edith said as she took a seat. "I have only a few minutes. My husband is gathering some men to arrest you. They'll be here soon."
Miles winced at the words "my husband," but he pulled a chair closer to hers. Edward, who was still standing, cleared his throat.
"Oh, Your Majesty!" Miles sprang from his seat. "I should have let you sit down first."
Miles quickly moved another chair next to his own. Then he remained standing until Edward was seated. Edith watched the whole scene with a puzzled look but didn't comment.

Finally, when Miles was seated once again and gazing devotedly at her, she began to speak. "I've come to warn you that you must leave at once. Not only did you attack my husband, but you are a threat to everything he has. It's especially dangerous for you because you look so much like our Miles."
"But I am Miles!"
"I know you think you're Miles." Edith paused. "And by the respectful way you address your friend, you also think he's the king."
"But I am the king!" Edward cried.

Edith ignored Edward. "If you didn't look so much like Miles," she went on, "my husband might leave you alone. But now he'll deny that you're his brother. No one will dare to challenge him because he holds power over everyone who lives nearby."

"Of course that's what the scoundrel will do." Miles knelt before Edith and took her hand. "And if you deny knowing me, then everyone who is dependent on Hugh will do the same. But if you say you know me . . ."
Edith blushed and pulled her hand away. "Apparently you still don't understand the danger. My husband is a tyrant who shows no pity. He'll destroy you!"
Edward burst out laughing. "Obviously you haven't seen Sir Miles in action. He's the bravest knight in my kingdom! Hugh is the one who should be afraid."
"Thank you for those kind words, Your Majesty," Miles said.
"If it's lack of money that's keeping you here, take this." Edith held out a purse to Miles. "Escape while you can, poor man. It's a matter of life and death!"
Miles waved away the purse as he stood up. "I want only one thing. Look me in the eye, Edith, and answer this question: Am I Miles Hendon?"
Edith looked steadily at him. "No, I don't know you," she said quietly.
"I can't believe this!" Miles said.
Before she could reply, several men burst into the room. They dragged Miles and Edward off to jail.
Edward and Miles were put into a cell together. Edward stood at the bars, calling for the guard, while Miles sat sadly in a corner.
"I demand to be released!" Edward shouted. "You have no right to imprison me! I'm the king!"
"And I'm the emperor!" a prisoner in another cell shouted. There were roars of laughter from other prisoners.
Edward went over to sit on the floor beside Miles. "How are you feeling?"
Miles sighed. "I thought everyone at Hendon Hall would be happy to see me. Instead no one seemed to recognize me, and I wound up here. I don't know whether to laugh or cry."
Edward put an arm around his friend. "You always get us out of trouble, Sir Miles. Maybe we can escape?"
But Miles was too discouraged to try. He spent the rest of the day thinking about Edith.
"I'm sure Edith recognized me," he said to Edward as they ate dinner. "But something—or someone—made her lie."
"There's only one thing I'm sure of." Edward made a face as he swallowed a spoonful of brown glop. "This is the worst food I've ever tasted."
The next day an old man carrying a basket came to visit all the prisoners. He handed fresh bread into each cell.
"Blake Andrews! My former servant!" Miles cried happily. "You must recognize me!"

"Shh!" Blake looked around to be sure no one was listening. "Thank goodness you've returned. I never believed you were dead, so when I heard you were here, I had to see for myself." Blake patted his basket of bread. "That's why I'm paying a charitable visit to the prisoners."
"Clever man!" Miles reached through the bars for some bread. "Now tell me what's been going on."

Blake explained that soon after Miles' brother Arthur died, Sir Richard became ill. "When your father received the letter about your death, he lost his will to live. He urged Hugh and Edith to marry before he passed away."
"And she obviously agreed to that." Miles shook his head sadly.
"No, she didn't!" Blake flashed Miles a triumphant smile. "She always believed that you'd return, so she resisted your father and Hugh's attempts to set a wedding date."
Now it was Miles' turn to smile brightly. "That's my Edith!"
Edward broke off a piece of bread. "So, how did she end up marrying Hugh?"
"She finally gave in when Sir Richard was on his deathbed," Blake said. "And she's been unhappy ever since."
"Oh, my darling Edith!" Miles whispered.

Blake leaned close to the bars and spoke softly. "It's rumored that after the wedding, she found a rough draft of that letter in Hugh's desk. She accused Hugh of rushing the wedding—and causing Sir Richard's death—by writing the letter himself."
"I can believe that," Edward said.
"As soon as Sir Richard died, Hugh began treating everyone cruelly—the servants, the villagers, anyone who depended upon him." Blake hesitated for a moment. "Even Edith."
This was too much for Miles, who grabbed the cell bars and tried to shake them. "I'll rescue Edith, if it's the last thing I do!"
The next day Blake returned with more bread and more news.
"The king will be crowned later this week," Blake said.
Edward pulled on Miles' sleeve. "We have to go back to the city right now!"
"I've heard that the king has an illness that affects his mind," Blake went on.
Edward glared at the old man. "The king is in perfectly good health! I command you to stop this gossip right now!"
Blake gestured toward Edward. "What's the boy talking about?"
Miles shook his head. "It's not important."
"Well, at least the king is kind and merciful," Blake said. "He spared the Duke of Norfolk's life, and now he's abolishing laws that oppress the poor."
"Who is this king?" Edward thought. "Even if Tom tried to pass himself off as me, he couldn't keep up that act for long."
Blake returned to the subject of the coronation and said Hugh would be attending. "He hopes the king will make him an earl because Hugh is friends with Lord Hertford."
Edward started at the name of his adviser. "We'll see about that!" he said.
After Blake left, two more prisoners were put into the cell. When Edward learned they were wrongly accused of crimes and sentenced to death, he was outraged.
"Miles, we have to get to the coronation," he whispered excitedly. "After I'm crowned, I can pardon these men and save their lives!"
Miles patted Edward's head. "First Blake's stories," he thought, "and now these fellows' tales of woe. I'm afraid everyone's stories have made Edward's illness worse!"
At last Miles and Edward had their day in court. The judge asked them to state their full names.
"King Edward."
The judge looked at Edward. "Would you like to try again, young man?"
Edward shook his head. "Not really."
The judge sighed and moved on to Miles. "And you? I suppose you're another member of the royal family?"
"No, I'm Miles Hendon."
The judge sighed again. "You do know that you're on trial for claiming to be Miles Hendon and the rightful owner of Hendon Hall? As well as for pushing Hugh Hendon?"
Now it was Miles' turn to sigh. "Yes."
During the trial Hugh described Miles as a "dangerous beggar," and Miles had to be restrained from pushing him again. The judge sentenced Miles to sit for two hours in the stocks.
"As for you," the judge said to Edward, "I'm tempted to give you the same punishment for being in such bad company. You should know better than to associate with such a rough criminal."
"He's not a rough criminal! He's my friend and a knight—"
"Enough!" Miles silenced Edward.
"As I was saying," the judge said to Edward. "I hope you've learned your lesson. If I find you making trouble again, you'll go straight to the stocks."
Edward muttered under his breath while Miles sent him frantic signals to be quiet.

Miles was led to the stocks in the village square with Edward following along for support. As soon as Miles sat down, people began to mock and insult him. When someone hurled an egg at Miles, that was too much for Edward.
"Shame on all of you!" Edward cried. "This is my servant and a knight in my court. Set him free. I am—"
"Edward, stop!" Miles shouted. "You'll only get yourself in trouble." Then he called to the sheriff, who was staring at Edward. "Pay no attention to the lad. He's ill."
The sheriff approached Edward. "You need to mind your manners. A couple hours in the stocks might straighten you out."
"Let's make it six," said Hugh, who had arrived to watch Miles suffer.
The sheriff grabbed Edward and started to drag him over to the stocks. Edward was so shocked that he couldn't even protest.
"Let him go!" Miles shouted. "I'll sit here for six more hours in his place."
"No!" Edward screamed. "Don't—"
"I'm warning you, lad," Hugh said. "For every word you utter, your friend will spend another hour in the stocks."
Because of his own punishment and Edward's, Miles spent much of the day in the stocks. At one point Edward approached him with a small branch. The young king touched him lightly on each shoulder.
"You are now an earl," Edward said to his friend.
Miles couldn't help but smile at this honor. And his hours in the stocks gave him plenty of time to think about what to do next.
"Should we return to the city?" he wondered. "I'm going to need someone powerful to help me before I challenge Hugh again. But where can I find someone like that?"
After about four hours, Miles thought of a possibility. "Blake said the new king was kind and merciful. Maybe I could talk to him, but would he believe the word of a penniless stranger?"

Miles thought some more. "My father had a friend at court, Sir Marlow. He was in charge of King Henry's kitchen or stables or something. Maybe he could help me. Yes, that's it! We'll go to the palace, and I'll ask Sir Marlow for help."
When Miles was finally released, he was ordered to leave the village. He wanted to go to the palace but had second thoughts about taking Edward back to the city.
"Edward keeps insisting on going to the coronation," Miles thought as they left the square. "Who knows how the excitement will affect his illness? What will happen when he's not crowned?"
But there was no discouraging Edward, who'd been busy planning his return. "By my calculations," he said happily, "we should arrive on the night before the coronation."

And that's exactly what happened. Miles and Edward arrived at night to find the city already celebrating. But Edward hadn't anticipated what would happen next. As they approached the bridge, Miles and Edward lost each other in the crowd.

Edward made his way to the cathedral where the coronation would take place. Dressed in rags, hungry and tired, the real king stood near the door. Watching workers streaming into and out of the cathedral, he waited for just the right moment. Then Edward slipped into the cathedral behind a carpenter and found a hiding place.
During the time that Edward was away from the palace, what had happened to Tom? Did he ever think about Edward, the real king?

At first Tom did think about the young prince who had treated him so kindly. But every day brought Tom a new and more exciting experience. His confidence increased until he no longer feared being discovered as an imposter. So Edward gradually faded from Tom's mind. When the day of the coronation arrived, Tom was happy in his role and looking forward to being crowned.
The day began with a grand parade through the city. Wearing a splendid outfit, Tom waved to the crowd from a white horse.
"This is all for me!" he thought proudly. "A few weeks ago, I would have hated all the attention. Today I didn't even mind that it took lots of servants three hours to dress me!"
As Tom scanned the crowd, he suddenly spotted his best friend from Offal Street.
"Oh, I wish I could wave and Julian would recognize me!" Tom thought wistfully. "Julian would be so surprised to learn that his old friend is about to be crowned king—for real!"
However, Tom also knew that if Julian did recognize him, his reign might be over.
"Good-bye, Julian," Tom said quietly without waving.
Lord Hertford rode up beside Tom, interrupting his thoughts.
"This is quite a day, Your Majesty," Lord Hertford said. "The weather is perfect, and your people are delighted to see you smiling and looking so well."
Lord Hertford handed Tom a small leather pouch. "Here's some money for you to toss to the people."
Tom reached into the pouch and threw some coins to the crowd. A loud cheer went up, and Tom happily waved. He was just about to toss more coins, when he noticed a familiar woman staring at him.
"Mother!" Tom thought. His hand flew up to his face, covering his eyes with the palm out.
Recognizing the gesture that Tom had always made when startled, his mother ran toward him.
"Oh, Tom, my dear son!" she cried. "I knew I'd find you if I kept looking!"
Tom barely glanced at her as he rode on. "I don't know you, woman!"
A guard grabbed Tom's mother and pushed her back into the crowd. "Get away from the king!"
Tom's heart broke to see his mother treated like that, but what could he do? He turned in the saddle for one last glimpse of her. She seemed brokenhearted, and he was filled with shame.
After exchanging clothes with Edward, Tom had thought about his mother and sister, Nancy, every day. But eventually he had forgotten about them, just as he had forgotten Edward.
"What's the point of being king if I must pretend that I don't know my own mother?" Tom thought. "I wish I'd never gone inside the palace. I don't want to be king anymore!"
The parade wound its way through the streets toward the cathedral. People cheered and applauded, but the king rode with his head bowed. He kept seeing his mother's face and how wounded she'd looked.
"Money! Give us money!" someone called out.
"Long live King Edward!" someone else cried.
But those voices were drowned out by the ones in Tom's head. He kept hearing his mother calling his name, and then his own voice saying, "I don't know you, woman!"
As Tom rode along, unsmiling and slumped in the saddle, people began to notice that something was wrong.
"The king doesn't look so good," one woman said to another.
"Maybe the rumors about his health are true," the second woman said.

"Your Majesty, this is not the time for daydreaming," Lord Hertford said. "People see your unhappy face and take it as a bad omen for your reign. You must sit up straight and smile! Toss them some more coins."
Tom did as he was told, tossing coins and smiling. But there was no longer any joy in his smile or his heart. Just before they reached the cathedral, Lord Hertford had to remind him of his duty.
"Come on, sir!" Lord Hertford urged Tom. "You've let some dreadful pauper upset you. Forget about her and think about this: you're about to be crowned king!"
"She isn't just some pauper," Tom said in a flat voice. "She's my mother!"
"Oh no!" Lord Hertford was so shocked that he pulled his horse to the side of the road.
"I'd hoped that the king was cured," he thought. "But instead his illness has obviously returned. What a terrible day for this to happen!"
Wearing a gold robe over his clothing, Tom sat on the throne in the cathedral. He grew more miserable with every minute of the coronation ceremony.

At last the great moment arrived. The archbishop lifted the crown and held it over Tom's head. Everyone was so busy watching the ceremony that no one noticed a boy in rags. He stepped from behind an old tomb and walked up the aisle.
"Stop!" Edward shouted. "I forbid you to crown him! I am the king!"
Tom stood up as a guard grabbed Edward's arm.
"Let go of him!" Tom commanded. "He's telling the truth! He is the king!"
Lord Hertford was as startled as everyone else but quickly recovered. "Unfortunately, His Majesty is ill again. Pay no attention to him and throw that pauper out."
"Touch him again, and you'll be thrown out!" Tom said to the guard.
The guard let go of Edward, who continued walking up the aisle. As Edward reached the throne, Tom fell on his knees.
"Let Tom Canty be the first to swear allegiance to you, my king."
Lord Hertford could not contain his surprise. "You two look exactly alike! If you don't mind, sir," he said to Edward, "I'd like to ask you some questions."
"Certainly," Edward replied.
Lord Hertford quizzed Edward about the court, the palace, King Henry, and Princess Elizabeth. Edward was able to answer everything correctly.
"Impressive!" Lord Hertford said. "But someone could have helped you learn the right answers."
Tom remembered how Marlow had helped him do just that.
"I'm not convinced that you're Edward," Lord Hertford said. "If only there was another way to test you . . . Wait! I've got it! Where is the Great Seal? Only the real King Edward knows this."
"I have no idea where it is," Tom said, trying to be helpful.

"Oh, that's easy! Where's my whipping boy?" Edward looked around until he spotted Marlow. "Take a carriage to the palace. You'll find the seal in a hidden compartment in my room. A servant will open the compartment for you."
Marlow hesitated to obey this boy who was dressed worse than he was.
"What are you waiting for?" Tom said. "You heard King Edward."
Marlow ran down the aisle.
The cathedral buzzed with chatter as everyone waited for Marlow's return.
"I think the pauper is the real king," one man said to another. "He picked Marlow out of the crowd."
"Yes, but he didn't know that Marlow is no longer a whipping boy," the second man said.
At last Marlow returned—with empty hands.
Lord Hertford shook his head. "I don't understand how anyone could lose something as big as the Great Seal. It's a heavy disk, made of gold—"
"Wait!" Tom shouted. "Are you talking about a round thing with lettering on it?"
Both Lord Hertford and Edward nodded.

"If only you'd described it like that, you could have had it awhile ago," Tom said to Lord Hertford. Then he turned to Edward. "The day we met, you hid it before you left. Tell everyone here where you put it."
Edward thought and thought while Tom grew increasingly nervous.
"Remember," Tom said, "we talked about our families and what I did with my friends. We traded clothes and looked in the mirror."
With every hint, Edward nodded in agreement.
"And then you noticed that the guard had injured my hand." Tom held it up. "Look, you can still see a faint bruise. You wanted to scold the guard, but first—"
"Oh, now I remember!" Edward cried. "Marlow, go to my room and look inside an armored glove on the table."
"Yes!" Tom hugged Edward. "That's it."
When Marlow returned with the Great Seal, Tom grinned. "And now, my king, it's time for you to be crowned."
Everyone in the cathedral applauded.
Lord Hertford waited for the noise to die down before addressing Tom. "And you—whoever you are—will be sent to prison for impersonating the king!"
"No!" Edward cried. "I owe my crown to Tom. He could have said nothing and continued as king. Instead he helped me remember where the Great Seal was. Sit down, Lord Hertford."
Lord Hertford sank into a seat.
"And one more thing," Edward said to everyone. "I've heard wonderful reports of Tom's brief reign. I can only hope to be as good a king as he has been."
Tom removed the gold robe and placed it over Edward's shoulders.
"By the way," Edward whispered, "how did you know where the Great Seal was?"
Tom turned red and confessed. "I was using it to crack nuts!"
The boys laughed together. Then the coronation ceremony resumed, and Edward was crowned king.

The day after the coronation, Miles stood outside the palace. He'd searched for Edward for two days but couldn't find the boy. So, Miles decided to seek help from his father's friend who worked at the palace.
Just then Marlow came through the gate.
"Do you work at the palace?" Miles asked. "Do you know Sir Marlow?"
"That's my father!" Marlow exclaimed.
"Tell him that Miles Hendon, son of Sir Richard Hendon, urgently needs to see him."
"Unfortunately, my father died last year," Marlow explained. "But I know someone who can help you."
Marlow led Miles into the palace courtyard and told him to wait.
Shaking his head in disbelief, Marlow hurried into the palace. "The king sent me to look for his friend. And there he was—right outside!"
As Miles leaned against a wall, a guard approached him.
"What are you doing here?" the guard said. "We can't have loafers around the palace!"
Suddenly Miles remembered Edward's note in his pocket and handed it to the guard. He'd forgotten about it amid all the trouble with Hugh.
"This ought to help me," Miles thought.
But the guard's face clouded over as he read the note. "Not another fellow claiming to be the king! I'm arresting you for—"
"For nothing!" Marlow hurried over to the guard and stopped him. Then he turned to Miles, bowed respectfully, and said, "Please come with me, sir."
Miles followed Marlow into a room where a line of people stood waiting to speak to the king. When the king looked up, Miles gasped.
"Is that my young friend?" Miles rubbed his eyes. "There's only one way to be sure."
Miles went over to a chair and sat down. Instantly a guard was at his side.
"You can't just come in here and sit down!" the guard said loudly.
The king laughed. "Oh yes, he can. This is Sir Miles, my trusty companion, and he's allowed to sit whenever I'm sitting. Hello, Miles, how are you today?"
"Very well, Your Majesty, though I'm surprised to see you here." On the outside Miles was laughing but inside he was embarrassed.
"I can't believe I bragged to King Edward that we have seventy rooms and thirty servants at Hendon Hall! That's nothing compared to what he's used to."
Struggling to believe Edward was really the king, Miles stared at the boy. " This is my pauper? This is the boy I vowed to protect?" Miles thought. "He has guards and a whole army to protect him!"
Miles stepped forward and bowed to the king. Then he stood aside while Edward scanned the people waiting to speak to him. The king spotted some people he recognized and beckoned them forward.
Miles drew his breath in sharply as Hugh and Edith approached the king. When Hugh asked to be made an earl, Edward's face hardened.

"You don't deserve the honor. Miles and I spent time in jail, thanks to you, and Miles spent time in the stocks." Edward called a guard. "Arrest this man. I strip him of his stolen title and property."
"I didn't know you were the king!" Hugh protested as he was led away, but Edward was no longer paying attention.
"Now, Lady Edith, you can tell me the truth," King Edward said kindly. "Did you recognize Miles at Hendon Hall?"
Miles held his breath, waiting for Edith's response.
"Yes," she said quietly. "My husband told me to lie and threatened to punish me if I didn't. When I said I didn't care, he threatened to hurt Miles."
"My Edith was trying to protect me!" Miles said fondly.
"I banish Hugh from my kingdom forever!" Edward declared. "Next!"
Tom stepped forward and bowed to the king.

"Tom Canty!" Edward smiled. "As a reward for taking care of my kingdom, you shall become head of the home for poor, abandoned children. You're welcome to live there with your mother and sister. Have you found them again?"
"Yes, Your Majesty, and I apologized to my mother for pretending not to know her," Tom said. "I wasn't quite myself, as you know, sir."
"I understand." King Edward smiled.
That day Edward wanted to arrest John Canty for cruelty to his family, but no one could find him.
In the years that followed, Hugh died in prison, which freed Edith to marry Miles. Tom became good friends with the king and was often seen at court. As for King Edward himself . . .
Whenever someone complained that he was too kind to the poor, he told a story. It was the tale of how he, a prince, had become a pauper.
"And that," he always said, "has made me a better king!"
